reviewText: Overrated?  Yeah right.  While this album isn't a classic by far, it still is no where near horrible.... "Kiss Tha Game Goodbye" is a very good album.  The first song (skippin the intro) is the best song on the album.  "Jada's Got A Gun" is a premier way for Jadakiss to show off his talent, which he has plenty of to go around."We Gon Make It" is another definite banger.  The beat isn't new, but the lyrics are definitely on point.  "Uh-hhh" is another great song.  Jadakiss rips up Beanie Sigel, with help from DMX, who sounds like he's also takin shots at another self-proclaimed "King" of the rap industry (Jay-Z)Overall, this album doesn have a few bad moments, but the good overshadows the bad.  This is a well-rounded album and hopefully Jadkiss won't keep his fans waiting so long for another round.

reviewText: I'll be among the first to admit I had not expected My Morning Jacket to be so versatile and fearless. For "Evil Urges" MMJ might want to call themselves Coat of Many Colors as the band breaks from expectations offering a patchwork of tunes that are all across the board yet still mesh quite well.Though folks will likely react most strongly to the stylized Princely romp of Highly Suspicious, the acoustic daydream embodied by Librarian strikes me as the more amazing departure. With a forays into `70s soul music on Thank You Too and the kinder, gentler `60s rooted Two Halves, MMJ put more distance from their image as just classic guitar rockers---albeit great ones---before pulling you back in with the one-two power punch that end the CD, Smokin from Shootin and Touch Me I'm Going To Scream Part 2.All in all, Jim James and his band mates deliver a classic summertime album, clearly having fun while stirring up enough dust from the fallow ground they have left behind heading on a flight of fancy that will get folks talking and keep people listening.

reviewText: After realizing the true meaning of the word "chemistry" upon my 1st full listen of Christina Milian's 3rd album "So Amazin'" & not to mention my seriously careless misuse of the words "classic" and "standout" on my previous review, I decided to give "Todd Smith" a clearer, more focused listen to his new music, resulting in my final decision...While this album may not be a Hip-Hop Classic, "Todd Smith" is a classic album in its own right, catering much more to the ladies & the mainstream audiences than many of his earlier projects.Like all albums of this generation & those before it, there are a few standouts to be found here & there throughout the album. "We're Gonna Make It", featuring underappreciated R&B;/Soul/Gospel artist Mary Mary, is a soulful, uplifting rapper/singer collaboration about persevering through the ups & downs life gives to you. "I've Changed", featuring Ryan Toby of City High fame, plays out like a heart-wrenching drama, illustriously painting the story of a man searching for forgiveness & redemption for the unfaithful crimes he committed on his girl. The classy afternoon love of "Favourite Flavour" -featuring the soulful vocals of multi-talented Hip-Hop/Soul Queen Mary J. Blige- & the emotionally raw power of 2nd single "Freeze" -featuring the uncompromising singer/songwriter Lyfe Jennings- also shine brightly on the album.Unfortunately, "Todd Smith" has its disappointing filler like every other album out there. The record-breaking smash hit single "Control Myself" -featuring the sexually charged, playful vocals of Jennifer Lopez- is totally tight in every aspect of the word (especially in terms of rapper/singer chemistry), but the song just feels so dated, and it's hard to imagine this song blasting through clubs, bedrooms or even I-Pods in the next few years. "#1 Fan", LL Cool J's only solo attempt on the album, is also a major disappointment, with LL Cool J attempting a Latin accent in his rhymes, but failing miserably. "It's LL & Santana" has a great beat to it, but regardless of the cocky bravado of Juelz Santana & LL Cool J, the chemistry doesn't work well when you put a Hip-Hop icon next to a B+ newcomer like Juelz Santana.The album's most confusing track to me, however, is the gangsta playa vs. ghetto chick track "Preserve The Sexy" -featuring "Princess of The Roc." Teairra Mari. While their musical chemistry & general public image make their chemistry unbelievably effective (Hip-Hop icon vs. Roc-A-Fella Princess/rough-core voice of a young female generation), it's hard to believe that LL Cool J would try hitting on someone almost half of his own age. It's kinda creepy, but the song works nonetheless, and is a clear favourite of mine. The beat is unsurprisingly tight as well.Altogether, "Todd Smith" is a classic effort, and although there are loads of guest appearances, each appearance adds more variety & flavour to the album. Not only that, but LL Cool J's legendary status in the world of Hip-Hop gives automatic street credibility to all guest performers on the album. The only artists that really fail to take full advantage of their opportunities are Juelz Santana & Jamie Foxx (on the inspirational "Best Dress", another great track) , which is a real shame, considering that both of them are some of the many newcomign talents I've enjoyed on their earlier work.Another problem with this album is its lack of thug joints. "What You Want" -featuring Freeway- is a typical, engaging, energetic Hip-Hop track about materialism, but it could've been better if he put A LOT more balance between his lover man joints & thug joints. Either way, the album's great, so GO BUY IT!
summary: LL Cool J + Diversity + Appropriate Guests = CLASSIC OF A DIFFERENT KIND!!

Whats the point of playing a 7 string guitar when you can't even play with 6?All in all, I had high expectations for this band and they totally let me down. reviewText: Fountains of Wayne are definitely independent thinkers. Life in a cover band, impressing girls with tattoos, going to the laser show, the most depressing prom theme imaginable ...these are not your average topics for any band. But not only do fountains of Wayne approach things in a different way, but they do it with melodies you can actually hum. This is a talented, intelligent band that will probably be stuck with that "critic's darling" label forever, ("Stacy's Mom" Not withstanding...and not on this CD!) but they deserve greater success. Sure there are a few misfires, like the repetitive "Hat and Feet," and the dated lyrics of "Go Hippie." But overall, you'll find yourself well-rewarded by this band's work.

reviewText: This debut from New York's southside Jamica, Queens crew led by Mr. Cheeks has made boyz with their hustlin', partying, street grooves on Legal Drug Money.  With memerable, catchy hooks and freestyle rhymes the Lost Boyz had themselves an almost classic.  Their party, upbeat joints like "Music Makes Me High" and "Get Up"  are what makes this such a hot commodity.  On the other end of the spectrum we have "Renee".  This is a song mourning over a death.  Besides, Mr. Cheeks uses the word love and keeps it raw and hardcore.  Member Freaky Tah also represented on here with Mr. Cheeks and with a solo song, "1,2,3".  Going back to their most obvious freestyle flow, listen to the two of them on "All Right".  A couple more upbeat tracks would have absolutely made this a classic.

reviewText: The singing, that is. This isn't a terrible album, but it certainly is missing a je ne sais quoi.Pros: The classy orchestrations remind me of the classic Sinatra-Jobim collaboration. Diana's Jobim-like single-note piano solos are the essence of wit and understated grace.Cons: Krall's singing has always been her weak point. Technically, her voice sounds good, but that's the problem. It's technically cool and precise, feathery, light, and on key. But it doesn't really touch me, except on personal material such as that found on The Girl In The Other Room. And some of the quieter material from her Paris concert. I'm not feeling it.Not only that, Quiet Nights is filled with tempos that are maybe just a bit to slow to begin with, and Diana often sounds like she needs to get some sleep or lay off the 'ludes.You're My Thrill is almost laughably bad, so ineffective is Krall at generating any kind of heat. Her delivery on So Nice sounds like she's doing a run through of the sheet music for the first time. What was she thinking? Not nice at all. Her slinky singing on Hang My Tears Out To Dry shows a little bit of the impishness and playfulness we see in her smile on the CD cover photo. What went wrong on the other songs, I can't guess.And the orchestrations do tend to get lush to the point of syrupy or schmaltzy in spots. Part of that is used to good effect, but sometimes it goes overboard.By contrast, Krall shines on Bacharach's Walk On By and How Can You Mend A Broken Heart by the Brothers Gibb. She sounds engaged here, and the arrangements are well thought out. Those two cuts are so good, it's almost shocking how dull some of the rest is. Corcovado (Quiet Nights) is one of my top ten favorite songs of all time, but Krall sleepwalks through the version on this album.Well, I'm sorry to say this CD is a step backward in her recorded output. Even as a relaxing cocktail music album it pales by comparison to The Look Of Love -- again, with the exception of the Bacharach and Bee Gees cover tunes.

reviewText: I have been listening to Joe since his debut in the 90's and while I've always been a fan of most of his music, some of his music left me wanting more.  It is no secret that All That I Am is one of Joe's defining efforts musically with Better Days coming in second in my opinion.  But none of Joe's efforts have hit me the way Signature does.  It seems that much of Joe's efforts had his signature sound but at the same time he was chasing some of the musical trends when it came to the uptempo numbers.  Hip Hop doesn't fit Joe in my opinion and on Aint Nothin Like me there was his share of hip hop.  Signature takes you on a journey back to Joe's signature style.  Some say it isn't classic, but I beg to differ.  I listened to this cd 4 times straight while doing work around the house and it is the first cd by Joe that I can actually say that I'm in love with.  In my opinion, better than anything R. Kelly has released in recent memory.  Every song is really good and for the sake of comparisons it is All That I Am part 2 in terms of lyrics and the mellow vibe.  It is Joe's signature sound that takes center stage.
summary: Joe is back to his Signature sound.

reviewText: "Transmissions..." is the record that showed the Flaming Lips were basically a great guitar pop band, albeit a very strange one. Sure, this is the one that has the big hit ("She Don't Use Jelly") but this is one of those albums that, cliched as it may sound, needs to be listened to in its entireity to really be appreciated. I'm not sure why, but I enjoy this album best during the late summer/early fall time of the year; something about driving around listening to "Turn it On" loudly brings back a certain carefree point in time. The skronk and squall of the Lips' earlier recordings is very much present, but the hooks are clearer and the songwriting seems less like the product of two-day LSD binges. Some of the best tracks here include the wistful "Superhumans," which hints at the pop majesty of the Lips' later work, "Pilot Can at the Queer of God" and the industrial-sized grooves of "Slow Nerve Action."

reviewText: It was a Tori Amos fan's dream!  A new studio disc and an 80-minute live collection all rolled into a nicely packaged into a two-cd set.  Both discs can be listened to over and over.  But the live disc is the one that draws the most attention.  For anyone who hasn't had the privilage of seeing Tori in concert is in for a treat.  It includes all of her trademark songs with increased length.  What really floors the listener is the 10-minute version of "The Waitress".  But if that's not enough.  The studio disc contains a very space-age material that Tori pulls off in all the glory that she's capable of giving a track.  My personal favorites on the first disc are: "Bliss", "Juarez", "Glory Of The 80's", "Joesephine", and "Concertina".  On the second disc I tend to favor: "Precious Things", "Cornflake Girl", "Space Dog", "The Waitress", and "Purple People".  The one place this album doesn't belong is in your car stereo.  It's far too easy to get lost in the music.

reviewText: I love the way that Raphael Saadiq combines vintage soul sounds with more contemporary influences. Saadiq has impressive songwriting chops and, as anyone familiar with his work with Tony Toni Tone knows, he has a lovely and versatile vocal style. Compared to the incredible "Instant Vintage", I thought "Ray Ray" was not as strong a set of songs. But he roared back with the mighty "The Way I See It" and now comes "Stone Rollin'," another solid set of tunes, some funky and some sly. From the opening song, the pounding "Heart Attack," to the moving final track, "The Answer," the heartfelt and energetic performances never falter. With this album  Raphael Saadiq is offering more lively bursts of soul that need to be heard by more listeners.

reviewText: When Aerosmith started to really crack down on their goal to become "America's Greatest Rock Band" (a journey started in 1971), they were quickly dismissed as "The American Stones."  High praise for some, it was meant to be derogatory, and Aerosmith meant to live past it.  Well, guess what?  No one calls them the American Stones anymore... and "Toys in the Attic," their first rock and roll hall of fame type record is the reason.  Though initally well-recieved because of the classic rock standards "Sweet Emotion" and "Walk This Way," "Toys" has lived well beyond the big singles as a solid, well-crafted piece of americana.Fusing blues, catchy tunes, and the band's regular dirty riffs and lyrics, they created their first 5 star album; one for the ages.  The tunes range from hobo-on-the-porch stories of "Uncle Salty," to the bluesy "No More No More," to the full metal "Round and Round," there are no losers in the 9 song set.  Not a weak moment to speak of.  And "You See Me Crying" is such R&B bliss, that when Aerosmith reformed for "Done With Mirrors," the band wanted to do a cover of it; that is until Joe Perry reminded them it was themselves."Toys in the Attic" is one of those rare albums that is equally strong track-by-track and in its entirety; it's regarded as a classic for good reason.  If you're a new Aerosmith fan (unlikely), start here.  Overall:  10 out of 10.

reviewText: This is the first Bette Midler cd I ever bought and what an introducion it was!  I was always scared off by her because of the sappy, by-the-numbers ballads she became famous for in the late 80's and to be sure there are a few of them on this set (4 to be percise), but for the most part she's doing crazy outrageous things that no one else can do.  A song about boxing?  She's got it.  A Hawiian ukulee song?  Done with charm and authenticity.  A comical song about living up others standards?  Never falis to make me laugh.  As do so many other tracks on this cd.  Whenever I'm in a down mood Bathhouse Betty is always there to pick me up.  Be it 'I'm Beautiful', 'I'm Hip', or 'Big Socks', you're sure to have a smile plastered on your face through out much of the set.  That is if you skip over the aforementioned ballads.  I don't enjoy her work on "moving" ballads.  The one exception being the lovely 'Laughing Matters'.  It manages to be poinent, honest and a bit comical all at the same time and her voice is in top form on it.For a good time grab Bathhouse Betty, she knows how to lift your spirits!

reviewText: One of the original OG's to spit pimp rhymes.  He been selling in the game now for at least fifteen years and has an ample supply of albums ( 14 or 15).  In many lists Too Short is not included as one of the greatest rappers ever.  Its a shame.  He constantly comes up with interesting stories and rhymes and combines tight beats and flow.  And more than that he has survived the game for 15 albums!!!!  He isnt underground rapper either.  He has too many collaborations to count and when he is on the song it makes it that much better. It's about Longevity not how many pop singles and jingles you can make up.  But I believe that the reason he doesn't get much play from the mainstream is because he is so explicit.  His detailed stories can be entertaining and disgusting at the same time which makes it tight.  That's not to say that Too Short relies on shock value its just that his main interest is sex.The beats on this album are extremely head-nodding and pimpalicious.  Only Too $hort can provide this type of beat.  His flows are on point and his rhymes are the same calibur pimp rhymes. The only reason this is not a five star album is because the hooks aren't all that great and some of the beats are less than stellar.  Plus Too $hort doesn't deviate from the sex talk so it can get tiresome sometimes.  If you are just now catching on that Too $hort is the man and you want a starting place try one of his other albums such as Cocktails or Get In Where You Fit In, or even Chase The Cat.  This cd is mainly for hardcore loyal fans and I doubt that many others would like it. Try his other albums before this one if you dont know.

reviewText: For me this album was Henley's high water mark as a solo artist.  The album was another huge hit that spawned several big singles and propelled the album well beyond platinum status.  This is one disc that deserved the sales in my opinion as every song on it is a winner.  Henley's social, religious and political commentary has never been more prevalent, and whether you agree with his points of view or not, the subject matter is always thought provoking.  Highlights of the disc include the opening title track which was co-written with Bruce Hornsby.  Bruce's signature piano is the main instrument of this tale of lost innocence in the Regan years of the U.S.  "I Will Not Go Quietly" is a rocking duet with Axle Rose from Guns And Roses.  "The Last Worthless Evening" is a cool ballad that was a big hit.  "New York Minute" was another big hit with great lyrics.  "Little Tin God" is Henley's reggae-ish take on religion.  "If Dirt Were Dollars" is another great lyric and one of the heavier rocking tunes on the disc.  The last track "The Heart Of The Matter" is  one of those relationship songs that came along at just the right time in my life.  This song always brings me back to my turbulent 20's, and relationships gone badly.  The lyrics pretty much reflected exactly what I was going through at the time, and it was like Henley got in my head and ripped this right out of my brain.  He does this type of song as well as anybody in my opinion.  Henley is once again supported by an all star cast of players.  The music is never overly adventurous, but fits exactly what Henley was trying to get across in most cases.  There are a few weak tracks here "How Bad Do You Want It?", "Shangri-LA", and "Gimmie What You Got" are all ok, but not up to the rest of the disc.  Overall though this is a very enjoyable album and the best of Henley's solo career.
summary: Don Henley - His Best Solo Album

reviewText: Alan Thicke is pretty much regarded as one of the great sitcom actors of our time. His portrayal of Jason Seaver is one of the great moments in american television. He was compassionate, caring and laugh out loud funny. His banter with teen superstar Kirk Cameron is what TV should be all about. I thought his real life son would be a lot like Kirk Cameron. Kirk Cameron is all that is right with the world. Robin Thicke is all that's wrong with music. I literally could not make it through four tracks of this album without wanting to throw my pop tart (cherry) against my kitchen wall as hard as I could. His singing is like fingernails on a chalkboard with vocals and instruments. Any comparison to Justin Timberlake is a huge insult to the man who followed me in bringing the sexy back. There is nothing on here that even approaches "What comes around" by JT.His voice reminds me of a time back in high school where we would go out and cruise dodge street for women. One of my friends had a ridiculous falsetto voice and when we would play some Michael Penn, he would sing his songs in this ridiculous voice. We eventually dropped him off at a bowling alley and never came back to pick him up. As most of the world knows, I front the supergroup Asschowder. The big difference between Robin Thicke and me is that I sing like a man. I can give edge to Celine Dion songs. The other difference is that my dad didn't star in an 80s sitcom. He made a guest appearance on Alf, but he was no Alan Thicke. The consolation to him is that I'm not Robin Thicke. He would disown me if I sang like that. Robin Thicke is well below average, while average asked me for my autograph again yesterday.

reviewText: Alice Cooper struck a universal chord with the title track from their fifth album and the group-penned anthem became the only Top 10 hit of their career--"School's Out" peaked at No. 7 in the summer of 1972.  [Note:  It was also a No. 1 hit for three weeks in the U.K.]While "School's Out" is the focal point (and only hit) of this apparent concept album, there are other classic Alice Cooper songs here, including the rockin' "Luney  Tune" (co-written by bassist  Dennis Dunaway and Alice Cooper), the snarling "Public Animal #9, and the jazzy "Blue Turk" (the latter two co-written by guitarist Michael Bruce and Alice Cooper). Two other strong tracks are the ones inspired by the music from WEST SIDE STORY:  "Gutter Cat vs. the Jets" and "Grande Finale." [It should be noted that Leonard Bernstein is given co-writer status on both of these tracks.]In addition to the terrific music, the original LP was housed in an album jacket that could fold into an actual school desk--and the record was not in a paper sleeve but a pair of pink women's underwear!  VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

reviewText: Weeks after its release and I'm loving MGMT's strange new sophomore album, Congratulations, more with each listen. I hear the Zombies influence, a few songs even making me daydream about a Zombies/Of Montreal collaboration. The vocals sometimes remind of disco-era Mick Jagger, but only if he had a little less Mick in his Jagger. They remind my girlfriend of Prince, which I also agree with. And their songs also remind me of this and that, as does their look and general approach and appeal. They're artsy pop music historians disguised as hipsters - the price young artists pay in 2010.All those familiarities we came to know on the band's debut, Oracular, are less obvious on Congrats. The sound here is also less instant, more clouded, expansive and odd, which led many reviewers to dismiss the record as inaccessible pop music upon its release. But wait, these songs are, for the most part, accessible as hell. Maybe not in an "Electric Feel" over-the-top sort of way, but this is definitely a poppy record full of hooks, riffs and fun, memorable moments. That the general vibe is so out there only makes the repeat button more interesting (and essential).So are these seemingly hip kids, as so many have said, simply getting weird to be cool in the face of stardom? That's not the feeling I get. I like to think that they - a then unknown band - made an uber poppy album (Oracular) so that they could later make an album like Congrats and have people actually hear it and think about it and talk about it and argue about it. From t-ball to the majors, and it worked. And they did a fine job of making credible pop a couple of years ago, their debut standing as one of the best pop records of recent memory. But now they're artists, making exceptionally weird music that is also somehow often accessible. I actually wish the new album was less poppy and more weird. I wish there were more 10-plus minute songs and freak-out moments. Less regard for pop structure and general of-the-time appeal.This shiny collection of left turns works because its makers are not just pop historians and perfectly capable musicians, but because, I'd suggest, the boys behind MGMT are genuinely strange people. Think 70s era Bowie. MGMT aren't the big box stars or Pitchfork heroes we once thought they would be. They're something else. They're adventurous, and this is an adventurous carnival ride of a record. I miss the extra punch producer David Fridmann offered on Oracular, but the production sound here is perfectly fine. Everything is perfectly fine - because none of it, not a single second, is predictable, boring or inauthentic. As it turns out, MGMT are the real deal; art freaks who deeply understand their craft and are pretty good at playing their instruments. With Congrats MGMT have become the rare bizarro pseudo-art band in this oversaturated Pitchfork era that deserves to release records.
summary: Destined to Be an Overlooked Gem

reviewText: Broken Bells is a side-project in-line with The Postal Service in terms of more comparisons than you think, especially quality-wise. Broken Bells is a melodic project that's sole purpose is to entrance you. Make no mistake, Bill 'Danger Mouse' Burton gives the band its great sound, but James Mercer of The Shins brings the heart of it. Without Mercer, Broken Bells is just a great piece of melodic work. But with Mercer, Broken Bells dives into the wonderland of dreamy wonder & enchantment so much, it should have been the soundtrack to Alice in Wonderland.Highlights Include:The High RoadVaporizeTrap DoorsThe Mall & MiseryThe album is relatively short at 35 minutes, but it feels like hours. But in this case, that's not a bad thing, since I never wanted to come down from the clouds that is this album's songs. Heck, when I first listened to the album, I fell asleep. Again, this is not a bad thing, since album lulled me with its melodic assault that you just want to lie in, and roll around, taking in all that's around you. The production values here are just off the chart. Everything just sounds so good, and every layer of instrumentation is played off perfectly. It's almost like a Chill album, except for the fact you welcome the vocals, since it completes the experience.Overall, I was really taken aback on how good this album was. There's so many layers working here, and most, if not all of them come together perfectly. It does things that should not work, but makes them a strength. It takes an album that could have worked solely on its instrumental work alone, but adds vocals that gives the album a soul. If you're a fan of melodic albums that en-trace you, or the current indie scene, then you should find much to love and savor here. If this is what broken bells sound like, then bells that are not broken, or are just fixed should be pretty extraordinary.
summary: Bells That Lull, Bells That Enchant, Bells That Lead You Down The Hole Into Wonderland

reviewText: You could sense the helplessness around London's clubs and bars as the much vaunted rock revolution gathered momentum. Who was England's representative? America, Sweden, Australia and for f***s sake even NZ had there's but England? Queue the Libertines. Street urchins from London's mean streets who have with the Clash's Mick Jones on the production helm made a raucous, gravely account of Urban decay and alienation.'Up the Bracket' is also quintessentially English. Taking in mountains of the Wedding present, the Jam and even a touch of Morrissey they swagger with a 'jack the lad' type arrogance. There's also, despite the chaotic clutter of their songs, melody's galore in this lot. Take 'time for heroes' which in another life may have been a Morrissey/wedding present collaboration. 'Boy's in the Band' rumbling and glorious all at once and then the closing tight fisted salute of 'I get along'.Decent folk of the world may ask "what hath god wrought??"  England at last has a worthy representative of the 'rock revolution' and we can all breathe a huge sigh of relief - the search is over.

reviewText: This is the cd I've been wanting Jewel to make ever since I heard her sing "Love me Just Leave Me Alone" on VH1 and thought "WOW this girl can ROCK!". Jewel's first two cd's ("Pieces of You" and "Spirit") both left me stale and I really can't listen to either of them but I am a fan of Jewel's music when it's treated right. Luckily, "This Way" is very close to being exactly that. Jewel doesn't bust out with a full rock album but she does give us some great melodies, brilliant songwriting, and catchy pop hooks ("Standing Still"). Songs like "Break Me" and "Jesus Loves You" are classic Jewel folk/pop while "Serve the Ego" and "I Won't Walk Away" are very atmospheric and has Jewel wrapping her deep beautiful voice around every part of the listener, it's a great experience. I'm enjoying every song on this cd except the title track which kinda leaves me with nothing...definatly pick up this cd!!!!

reviewText: "Tical O: The Prequel", the long-awaited third studio effort from the most popular emcee out of the Wu-Tang Clan, Method Man, was originally planned as a conceptial album that predated his first solo, "Tical". Def Jam has been pushing this one back since the fourth quarter of 2000. Was the wait worth it? Has Method Man finally put out a solo record worthy of his fans' expectations? More importantly, can he live up to the hype after a six-year dropoff since his last solo album?The biggest problem with "Tical O" is its title. Despite what Method Man has said in interviews, this album really doesn't show any signs of being a precursor to either of his albums. His sound is more advanced than his last record, many of the guests were unknowns in 1999, and the album seems to speak on a number of current topics. In the end, it really shouldn't matter as long as the album is hot. Problem here is even Method Man's finest work seems drowned out by the overproduced beats on this LP. There are the occasional tracks that stand-out like the first single, "What's Happenin" where Meth and guest rapper Busta Rhymes show a phenominal chemistry as they trade flows over a beat by DJ Scratchator. When his Wu brothers show up, it's all gravy as well. "The Turn" featuring Raekwon and produced by The RZA is one of just a short few tracks that actually make the grade. "Afterparty" with Ghostface is another. After that, it's more or less a collection of rather mediocre recordings. Meth's collabos with Missy Elliot on "Say What" and Ludacris on "Rodeo" seem like he's trying to fall back on a popular sound rather than put out a quality track. Even his collaboration with Redman and Snoop Dogg on "We Some Dogs" is rather lukewarm.The early response to "Tical O" has been mostly mixed. Some fans are calling for a boycott of Wu albums calling this the worst Method Man project ever while others stand in a state of denial calling it one of the year's hottest. They're both wrong. Reportedly, Method Man had originally recorded a different version of this album with production handled mostly by The RZA but Def Jam turned it down. It's too bad because it probably couldn't have been any worse than this one. That is not to say that Method Man totally dropped the ball here. Like I said earlier, "Tical O" has its moments but it's not packaged right. Those expecting a return to the "36 Chambers" days will be sorely dissapointed but if you're a hardcore Method Man fan then you might find a few tracks on here to your liking.

reviewText: I know I will lose some helpful reviews here, maybe maybe not, but This is the best Album Whitney ever released.  When this came out, I remember my mom and me rushing out to Target to buy it.  We paid like 10 bucks for the cassette, cuz we didn't graduate to CD's until 1993.  We played it all the way home, then rushed to continue it on the stereo inside.  We didn't dislike one track.  I still don't dislike one track here.  This was a Family Favorite until it was eaten up in the car's tape deck.  I cried that day.  My sister found me a copy of the CD at a garage sale for a quarter.  I was shocked at the price, and have had the same copy since 1995.  I cherish this album and here, I plan to share my thoughts of the songs, and how they are in my opinion...1)I'm Your Baby Tonight: A great tough opener, no more wanting to dance with somebody...only dancing she wants to do is in the sheets it sounds like...and for good reason, a good girl is only good for a while.  The temptation is too much to bare, hence the lyric "From the moment you touched me, I was ready to die...I've never been fatal, you're my first time" For a first single it was an across the board smash and lies very unappreciated in her catalog.2)My Name Is Not Susan: Another tough song, shedding the pop image attached to her from earlier dance hits.  This track has her angry again from matters of the heart.  The beat is once again strong and funky, still sounds fresh nearly 20 years later!3)All The Man I Need:  This was the first ballad single from the album, very brooding reminding me of at-the-time labelmate Jeffrey Osbornes 1990 Smash Only Human (Another album and song milestone of the year) where they tell a story, and have great vocal stylings throughout.  Brought her the 2nd #1 on the album, and more success for duet partner Kenny G.4)Lover For Life: Popular quiet storm radio aired track, that is gorgeous and midtempo.  A slight departure from the tough edge but definitely sexy and different, featuring some vibes playing, a gauzy airy synth and a fantastic sax solo from Gerald Albright.5)Anymore: A full blown dance song from Whitney and Babyface, features a fun call and response near the end "Sing It Face..." I used to adore this song when I was younger.6)Miracle: The only possible candidate for the shlock cannon is here.  A beautiful song but perhaps a little overdone, and over used (I had it on a Ford Audio Sampler, and played the song out, so my opinion is kind of biased) I do love the song, but it takes some getting used to, especially if you played it a lot at first, then tired of it afterward.7)I Belong To You: One of the reasons why Narada Michael Walden is such a great producer is because he writes dreamy songs for his artists (Check out Taylor Dayne's If You Were Mine, or Tevin Campbell's Brown Eyed Girl) Another mid tempo track, and the 3rd hit from the record.  This one is a scorcher8)Who Do You Love?: You can tell this one was written and produced by Luther.  Gospel edge, great hook, great bridge, and background vocals to die for.  The man was truly one of a kind, he should have produced more for her, this song is fun, and humourous!!9)We Didn't Know (Duet With Stevie Wonder): You can hear on this track that the pair recorded together.  They have such an emotion and chemistry.  Whitney compliments Stevie so well and vice versa.  The line "Best Of Friends...The Best" is sexy and sentimental all at once, and one fan wishes they had done more together.  Much more charisma than her cousin had with Wonder.10)After We Make Love: The lone track produced by Michael Masser, Houston's former right hand man.  Ended up being the second true ballad and wasn't released.  The song is beautiful, enhanced by an extreme amount of reverb, but not annoyingly so, with a mellow drum beat and vocal acrobatics, it's a song about losing your virginity...but a good one!11)I'm Knockin' : Another gospel influenced track, featuring CeCe Winans, this is a definite pot boiler, that starts sounding like another song to add to the dance pile, and adds on the charm at a very slinky breakdown, a very nice, simple close to an album very well done.In these years Arista records had their share of fierce talent, from Whitney, to Jeffrey Osborne, and Jennifer Holliday, as well as Curtis Stigers, Kenny G, and Lisa Stansfield, the label released so many quality albums that they had nothing but hits on their hands.  The fact that critics believed this was a stab for Whitney to gain street cred was just a tad rude, seeing as if you look at her now, it was no fluke that this sounded so genuine.  The record got a bad rap, a lot of the white audience disliked it (my dad and a few neighbors happily excepted) but hopefully this won't be looked at as the mess it has been named to be.  This will always be my favorite houston album and I stick by what i've written above. To me Houston through Hiatus, bad marriage, drug addiction and rage, has still managed to make good records, though becoming a tad more ghetto and or nervous in the process, I only hope she can surprise me as much as she did with 'I'm Your Baby Tonight'

A beautiful song but perhaps a little overdone, and over used (I had it on a Ford Audio Sampler, and played the song out, so my opinion is kind of biased) I do love the song, but it takes some getting used to, especially if you played it a lot at first, then tired of it afterward.7)I Belong To You: One of the reasons why Narada Michael Walden is such a great producer is because he writes dreamy songs for his artists (Check out Taylor Dayne's If You Were Mine, or Tevin Campbell's Brown Eyed Girl) Another mid tempo track, and the 3rd hit from the record. This one is a scorcher8)Who Do You Love?: You can tell this one was written and produced by Luther. Gospel edge, great hook, great bridge, and background vocals to die for. The man was truly one of a kind, he should have produced more for her, this song is fun, and humourous!!9)We Didn't Know (Duet With Stevie Wonder): You can hear on this track that the pair recorded together. They have such an emotion and chemistry. Whitney compliments Stevie so well and vice versa. The line "Best Of Friends...The Best" is sexy and sentimental all at once, and one fan wishes they had done more together. Much more charisma than her cousin had with Wonder.10)After We Make Love: The lone track produced by Michael Masser, Houston's former right hand man. Ended up being the second true ballad and wasn't released. The song is beautiful, enhanced by an extreme amount of reverb, but not annoyingly so, with a mellow drum beat and vocal acrobatics, it's a song about losing your virginity...but a good one!11)I'm Knockin' : Another gospel influenced track, featuring CeCe Winans, this is a definite pot boiler, that starts sounding like another song to add to the dance pile, and adds on the charm at a very slinky breakdown, a very nice, simple close to an album very well done.In these years Arista records had their share of fierce talent, from Whitney, to Jeffrey Osborne, and Jennifer Holliday, as well as Curtis Stigers, Kenny G, and Lisa Stansfield, the label released so many quality albums that they had nothing but hits on their hands. The fact that critics believed this was a stab for Whitney to gain street cred was just a tad rude, seeing as if you look at her now, it was no fluke that this sounded so genuine. The record got a bad rap, a lot of the white audience disliked it (my dad and a few neighbors happily excepted) but hopefully this won't be looked at as the mess it has been named to be. This will always be my favorite houston album and I stick by what i've written above. To me Houston through Hiatus, bad marriage, drug addiction and rage, has still managed to make good records, though becoming a tad more ghetto and or nervous in the process, I only hope she can surprise me as much as she did with 'I'm Your Baby Tonight'

reviewText: Joss Stone's a decent singer, but shouldn't be writing songs; or releasing them. I couldn't find a single memorable tune here. I also thought her singing was too flamboyant, but perhaps it's to keep up with the heavy production, which is so overcooked it's insufferable. Next time Joss should try losing the rappers and the big beat overkill. As one critic wrote, "Sometimes it takes more balls to go it alone then with a whole crew." I couldn't agree more. This album is like musical Kleenex, use it, then lose it. Better luck next time.On the other side of the coin, there's "The Orange Album" by Stefy (Rae) which is a stunning debut. Had Gwen Stefani made it, journalists would have called it a pop masterpiece. It's new artists like Stefy that could keep the music business afloat. Are we listening Ms. Stone.

reviewText: After putting out a great first album that was politically charged, 2pacalypse Now was criticized by the dumbest vice president that we ever had. Tupac made his valient return with this album to settle the score. The album starts off with a great single called Holla If Ya Hear Me(also off of The Above The Rim soundtrack) where Pac drops some gems. He also drops jewels in the form of Point The Finga, Soulja's Revenge and the title track. Keep Your Head Up was one the most beautiful odes to black women that I've ever heard. Papa'z Song is where Tupac and Wycked passionately talk about their deadbeat fathers. If you thought Pac wasnt going to address Dan Frail, guess again! He mentions him in Pac's Theme and in Last Wordz. Ice Cube and Ice T join in on Last Wordz and Threat joins in on Peep Game. I liked I Get Around feat Digital Underground but that song shouldnt be what Tupac is remembered by. There are two songs I dont care for. Guess Who's Back and Deadly Venomz(feat Treach, Apache and Live Squad). Other than that, this album is susperb. Bottom Line: Strictly 4 My N***** is a criminally slept-on album that showed the positive side of Tupac(you know the side that only a few real fans embrace him for). He showed that he was a force to be reckoned with while giving you gems that most rappers these days wouldnt dare do. His death is an unfortunate loss for hip hop but his music lives on. Standout Tracks: HOLLA IF YA HEAR ME, POINT THE FINGA, SOULJAH'S REVENGE, PEEP GAME, KEEP YA HEAD UP, STRICLY 4 MY N.I.G.G.A.Z., THE STREETZ R DEATHROW and PAPA'Z SONG.REST IN PEACE TUPAC AMARU SHAKUR.

reviewText: I don't know what to say about this CD except that it is beautiful.  With the exception of "A Space Boy Dream" every song is sublime.  The title track should have been a smash radio hit, but America has really lost the taste for quality in music.  This album reminds me of "Forever Changes" by Love.  It's not as loopy and psychadelic as that, but I imagine people in 2020 discovering this album and wondering how in the world was this not a hit?I guess the main reason I didn't give this 5 stars is that the album is a little too one speed.  It doesn't have a great rocker on it anywhere (probably not fair since they obviously weren't going for it).  But the album just never hits that one song that gets you all pumped up or choked up or fired up or whatever.  Nevertheless I wholeheartedly recommend this record.

reviewText: One may question whether Martin Page was a "one hit wonder" or not.  Prior to releasing his debut album, "In the House of Stone and Light", Page established himself as one of the best songwriters in the music industry.  Page was responsible for co-writing two of the great songs of the 1980s: "These Dreams" by Heart and "We Built This City" by Starship.  These songs peaked in 1985 and truly capture the essence of "1980s Music".  The two songs are very different.  For "These Dreams", Page co-wrote with acclaimed songwriter Bernie Taupin, a powerful and haunting ballad.  Page also teamed up with Taupin and J Geils Band front man Peter Wolf for "We Built This City".  While some malign this song, I still think this song was a terrific song and enjoy it even today (especially the guitar riffs done by Craig Chaquico - one of the most underrated guitar players in the music industry).  No doubt Page has proven himself to be a top songwriter.  In a way, it is logical for an acclaimed songwriter such as Page to strike out on his own and make his own album.  In 1994, Page would release "In the House of Song and Light".  While I wouldn't say this collection hits a homerun, it is a solid enough collection.  Page does a good enough job to warrant follow-up albums.  However, this was not to be - this would be Page's only album he would release.  While the title track would be the only big hit off of this collection, there still are other tracks that are just as solid."In the House of Stone and Light" would be released nearly a decade after the success of "These Dreams" and "We Built This City".  This was around the time the music landscape was changing and giving way to the rise of Alternative Rock.  Page's style does integrate keyboards into his sound, but I would categorize it as Adult Contemporary as opposed to Synth-Pop.  For "In the House of Stone and Light", Page continues his adult contemporary music.  For this collection Page writes all of the songs himself - except for two songs in which he brings back Taupin to collaborate with.  For the album, in addition to providing the lead vocals - Page plays multiple instruments such as Bass, Keyboards, and Guitars.There is a slight spiritual influence on this collection, but wouldn't say it's dominant.  You hear the influence on "In the House of Stone and Light", "Shape the Invisible", and "The Door".  Page also manages to add some sociological, romantic, and historical points to the songs as well.Here is a song by song synopsis of the collection:"In the House of Stone and Light":  This is the title track and is worthy of being the title track and was Page's "One Hit".  It is a solid track and I'm surprised Page didn't garner Record of the Year consideration.  Page not only brings a terrific melody to the table, but he brings some very passionate vocals to a well written song (listen to when Page sings "I will not rest till I lay down my head")  There are outstanding background vocals with Brenda Russell participating in that role."Shape the Invisible":  The intro has a slight Indian music theme to this.  The song then progresses into a "St. Elmo's Fire" sounding classic 80s style.  Phil Collins guests on drums."I Was Made For You": Keyboard-laden adult contemporary song.  Page demonstrates good vocals on this track.  Collins again guests on drums."Keeper of the Flame": This track hit the charts, but wasn't a big success commercially.  However this is a very good track - the Carribbean/reggae style music goes well with Page's vocals.  Page also demonstrates very good range in his vocals on this one."In My Room":  This is a softer track.  From a vocals standpoint it didn't excite me, but when you look at the lyrics - there is some real powerful stuff.  This song tackles the subject of domestic abuse."Monkey in My Room":  There is something about songs about Monkey's that are awesome.  Peter Gabriel did "Shock the Monkey" and George Michael did "Monkey".  Now Page does "Monkey in My Room" - co-written by Taupin.  Like Gabriel and Michael's version, Page's version brings an edge.  I've heard comparisons that this is a knock-off of Gabriel and Michael - I tend to disagree.  I feel this song provides a nice change of pace while still fitting into the adult contemporary mold."Put on Your Red Dress":  Another classic Adult-Contemporary song - and I loved the vocals on this one.  This is a song that involved a guy wanting to revisit romance.  This is a terrific love song.  You gotta love the reference to "St. George's Bay" (located in Newfoundland, Canada)."Broken Stairway": This the collection's shortest track.  This is another soft track.  This one didn't excite me too much - although Page does a nice job with the vocals."Light in Your Heart":  Another collaboration with Taupin.  Page shows another side to his vocals - proving he can provide ranges in his vocals.  This song has a slight mantra feel to it on the chorus.  Brenda Russell provides more background vocals and Phil Collins also provides the drums."The Door": This is a powerful song that deals with someone who was in a concentration camp.  The song is told in the form of a narrative.  This demonstrates showcases why Page is such a great songwriter.The liner notes include all of the lyrics as well as the musician credits and acknowledgements.  Overall, this is a very good collection.  It proves that Page is as good a vocalist as songwriter.  I'm kind of disappointed this is the only album that was released by Martin Page.  He certainly proved himself on this album.  Perhaps the only drawback is the style of the music was more 1980s than 1990s. Overall -  Highly recommended

reviewText: Every artist has a career album and this is Eric Clapton's.This CD is not only his personal best but one of the All-time Rock classics.The album is primarily blues and has alot of electric slide guitar on it. This album was put together in the studio over a period of months. The sessions were very long and often they would sleep right there in the recording studio.Duane Allman plays much of the slide on the CD.This CD includes the classics "Bell Bottom Blues, Key to the Highway, Have you ever loved a woman. Layla and a very strong version of the Jimi Hendrix classic "Little Wing". There is not a bad song on the entire CD. This will prove to be Eric Claptons' finest hour and still holds up to the test of time.This CD is a guitar lovers dream. He plays the guitar as only Eric Clapton can. If you like blues you will like this CD.

reviewText: Instead of continuing in dream pop territory, (which aside from "Lovefool" was yucky) the Cardigans dive into my favorite type of music!  Altnernative rock & trip-hop. "Higher" is too blah, and so is "Explode".  Ooooo, let's not forget another song that's a real treat, "Erase/Rewind"!  It's a cute and catchy song.  The instrumental at the end could of been good, but, it's too brief. If you adore the Cardigans previous work, you could easily be disappointed with this effort, but, if you've got some rockin' inside you'll bones, you'll enjoy it.  You may not think of the cardigans inside Mr. Rogers closet when you hear this, but, there's still plenty of soft fabric left.  lol, wasn't that a horrible ending?

reviewText: Godsmack's 2003 follow up to "Awake" may not be flawless, but its still a really good album. The set features the band's traditional rock sounds, only with a little more edge this time around. Just check out lead single "Straight Out Of Line" and you'll get the feel of the album. Many of the songs have the band focusing on hatrid and betrayal, such as the title track "Faceless" and "I ... Hate You". Other songs, like "Changes", do the same but with a different vibe. This time, Godsmack means business. The album also includes the hard-rocking anthem from the Scorpion King Sountrack "I Stand Alone" (this track is incredible live, i saw Godsmack with Breaking Benjamin and (hed) P.E a couple weeks ago, this track blew me away!). In all, this is the band's best effort, the last track, with the indian stuff at the beginning, totally sums up the album. The most angry, but yet the best, seems you'd find that predictable with Godsmack.

reviewText: The world over, Cat is known as a legend. Why? Simply because he wrote some of the most beautiful music. Where do you start if you are new to his music? This album, also known as 'Remember' in other countries, happens to  be a good place to start. Much, much more songs than on the original  'Greatest Hits' which I have also reviewed. It's nice to see a track from  his album 'Foreigner' here whichis an album overlooked on Cat compilations.  Although the track is only an excerpt, it is better than nothing. My  favourite track of all time 'Sad Lisa' is missing from this compilation.  Naturally, they can only fit so many on, but 'Sad Lisa' is one of his VERY  best, so it's omission does not go by unnoticed. 'Two Fine People' is also  missing, but there are still stacks of goodies on this album to please  everyone - Sitting; Morning Has Broken, Peace Train & Where Do the  Children Play. Worth having, and treasuring.

reviewText: Despite this album's reputation of being an 80's period piece, and, as everyone is probably aware of, their song Video Killed the Radio Star was the first video broadcast on MTV, this is an immensely catchy, tuneful, undated, surprisingly complex album.  Despite it being identified as "80's", it still sounds excellent and quite contemporary.  I didn't listen to this album when it came out, but when I finally got around to getting it, I found it absolutely charming and wonderful.The first two songs, Living in the Plastic Age and the deservedly classic Video Killed the Radio Star, set the tone.  They are electronic pop gems.  The synthesizers and computers never overpower Trevor Horn's wonderful vocals, and Geoffrey Downes's musicianship.  The lyrics are quite literate and intelligent (especially on Video), and you never think MTV or 80's when you hear this album.  I've actually never watched the entire video for Video Killed the Radio Star for the record.  Maybe I like the song too much and don't want it ruined.  This album has almost a prog rock vibe to it, dare I say.  It isn't surprising that Downes and Horn went on to join Yes shortly after this album on their unjustly trashed, much maligned album Drama (Drama is excellent).  The only other band that comes to mind that tried this intelligent computer pop/prog rock was Jethro Tull and Ian Anderson with Tull's Under Wraps and Anderson's hard to find but excellent CD/album Walk Into Light.  Mike Oldfield's Five Miles Out also falls into this category.Maybe The Age of Plastic is the missing link between prog rock and electronica.  Go ahead, call me pretentious.  Regardless of my possibly pretentious machinations, this is still an excellent CD/album.

It isn't surprising that Downes and Horn went on to join Yes shortly after this album on their unjustly trashed, much maligned album Drama (Drama is excellent). The only other band that comes to mind that tried this intelligent computer pop/prog rock was Jethro Tull and Ian Anderson with Tull's Under Wraps and Anderson's hard to find but excellent CD/album Walk Into Light. Mike Oldfield's Five Miles Out also falls into this category.Maybe The Age of Plastic is the missing link between prog rock and electronica. Go ahead, call me pretentious. Regardless of my possibly pretentious machinations, this is still an excellent CD/album.

reviewText: ROCK OF AGES is a great live album from The Band, especially considering that their previous studio album, CAHOOTS, received a lukewarm critical and commercial reaction. The group hired New Orleans R&B legend Allen Toussaint to arrange horn charts for this set, so some songs, notably "Chest Fever", sound somewhat different from their original versions. This is is most noticeable on that song and on others that originally appeared on MUSIC FROM BIG PINK, where five musicians did everything you hear. Still, this album wears even better than the great THE LAST WALTZ, where a full orchestra appears on some cuts.

reviewText: Six months after this recording was made, `King' Curtis Ousley would be stabbed to death while standing in front of his New York City apartment building. This tragic violence brought a premature close to a career that had recently projected to new heights, and seemed poised to go just about anywhere. Active since the early fifties, King Curtis moved easily from jazz to soul to rock and roll. To put things in perspective, you should know that when Sam Cooke sings "Play that one called `Soul Twist'" in "Having a Party," he's referring to a King Curtis tune. The man was ubiquitous, but usually stayed behind the scenes, serving as a bandleader, producer or back-up musician for an endless number of performers, including the Coasters, the Isley Brothers, Bobby Darin and John Lennon. In 1971, he was acting as bandleader for Aretha Franklin (see my review for "Aretha Franklin Live at the Fillmore West") and racking up a few hits of his own. "King Curtis Live at the Fillmore West" culls the highlights from his own sets at this venue, and it also marks a high point of his recording career.The band alone justifies the price of admission. Billy Preston plays keyboards and Cornell Dupree plays guitar, while Jerry Jemmott and Bernard Purdie make up the rhythm section. Fattening out the rich sound of Curtis' own baritone saxophone are the Memphis Horns, making this ensemble a dream team of funky soul-music brethren. Even when the material is lacking, the band manages to transcend mundanity with spirited interpretations. Would you expect "Ode to Billie Joe" to have a fatback groove? I wouldn't have.  Could you even imagine a baritone sax handling Robert Plant's vocal line for "Whole Lotta Love"? I didn't think so. This version in particular brings the song full circle, taking it closer to its roots as a Willie Dixon composition. The best tune here, though, is "Memphis Soul Stew," a gorgeous eight-minute rhythmic workout that virtually defines the funky/loose and yet stop-on-a-dime/tight spirit of contemporary soul music. It is a virtual primer in everything anyone would need to know about cooking up a hot rhythm and letting it simmer until it boils over with intense energy. Throw in a bonus track that features Billy Preston molding "My Sweet Lord" into something uniquely his own, and you will have to wonder how on Earth anybody could claim George Harrison's composition as a derivative of "He's So Fine."King Curtis had a lengthy career, but it still ended much too soon. Catch this set and you're also bound to wonder how soul music would have progressed had we not lost such a talented force at the peak of his powers. A-  Tom Ryan

reviewText: A masterpiece, superior to its predecessor which, don't get me wrong was very good.There is a relaxed, breezy feel to the whole cd, and the songs catch you instantly. The lead off single 'You don't know my name' is a brilliant song (co penned with Kanye West), reminiscent of classic 70s soul, complete with a spoken word section. In fact, the whole cd sounds like classics from the 70s, amazing to find that all but one of the songs are penned or co penned by Keys.On 'If I aint got you', 'If I was your woman' (an excellent remake by the way) and 'When you really love someone', she sings with a raspy growl seeping with passion, akin to Mary J bilge.Shock horror on seeing her work with Timbaaland (don't get me wrong, I love Timbaaland, but didn't think his futuristic funk would fit Alicia's smooth retro soul), but the result is the lovely retro funk of 'Heartburn'. All she needs now is an afro.'So simple' is simply fab and is my favourite, with delicate piano tinklings sprinkled throughout. 'Dragon days' is a corker, 'Diary', 'Samsonite man', the lovely interlude 'Feeling U, feeling me', and the jazzy 'Nobody, not really' are superb.Another good point, averaging 4 minutes, no song overstays its welcome (exception, 'You don't know my name' which needs all of its 6 minutes 6 seconds to weave its magic).There were few soul cds released in 2003 which can dream of coming close to this soon-to-be-classic. Awesome!!!

reviewText: Before I begin, let me make two points: 1. No, OutKast didn't break up, and 2. OutKast has NEVER been known for straight hip-hop (remember "Funky Ride" from Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik?) Aight then...André 3000 - The Love Below (Arista, 2003)There is hardly any rapping in this album except for "A Life in the Day of Benjamin André (incomplete)" (incomplete because André's life is still going!) which is an autobio of his rap life, "Roses" (with Big Boi), "Spread" and "Happy Valentine's Day". André is playfully singing in the other songs but the main focus is on his production and the lyrics (really listen to "Hey Ya!" to get the message). André talks about love, love lost, and the joys and pains of just being André. A classic. He truly is an outcast in the rap game. -EJRBig Boi - Speakerboxxx (Arista, 2003)Whereas André's album is the most creative, Big Boi's is the most solid. He also is a great producer, concocting the album's greatest track, "Reset" featuring Debra Killings as usual on vocals, Khujo of Goodie MoB and Cee-Lo formerly of Goodie MoB (no hard feelings between the latter two artists, I guess). This song brings back the smooth ATLiens sound to Big Boi's album while "GHETTOMUSIK", produced by André 3000, brings back the Stankonia sound complete with a boomin' bass beat and a Patti Labelle sample. I'm not mad that there are a lot of guest stars on Big Boi's album because every time I heard Big Boi rhyme, it's usually with someone else anyway. An example of this is on "Flip Flop Rock" featuring Jay-Z and Killer Mike, and although it's no "Poppin' Tags", the hook by Hova is catchy. Another classic album. -EJROverall, this is the great unconventional album that Common's Electric Circus should have been (in that review, I said to listen to that album until OutKast drops another album). Always depend on OutKast for original hip-hop.

reviewText: I guess if you want Morcheeba to keep cloning their earlier albums, this album will disappoint.  If FRAGMENTS reeked of insincerity that would be  one thing, but I don't remotely hear any lack of commitment here.  Often  I've found that when long-time fans start jumping ship--which has happened  with artists as diverse as Miles Davis and Cibo Matto--then that's about  the time I want to get on board, or renew my commitment to the artist if  I'm already a fan (as I am here).  Because that's usually when one finds  out for certain that the group has the convictions to challenge themselves,  to grow, to learn, to keep their ears and minds open, to not let themselves  get pigeon-holed into what they once were (often ironically by those who  profess to be their biggest and most loyal fans).Since when can't music  of depth and vision have an optimistic tone?  Do people still buy the  artist-must-suffer (and/or make us suffer) cliche?  To me, this album slams  home the potential of the first two albums, often packing an  old-school-bridged-to-Y2K funky vibe that would make George Clinton a proud  father.  And if you don't associate the P-Funk as an influence on Morcheeba  from the beginning (not so much the lyrics as the feel and attitude), I bet  they would confirm it...and even if they wouldn't, the music itself does.Yes, the surface is more inviting, with captivating melodic hooks and  rhythms that sometimes dance with the upbeat vigor of vintage 70s-80s funk.  But is that such a bad thing?  Funk is one of the most creative and  resilient pop culture idioms of the last century.  Beyond that, I still  hear a consistent underlying thirst for experimentation...there is too much  imaginative blending of styles and instrumentation to dismiss the results  as being some assembly-line attempt to sell more records.  I'd play this  alongside acclaimed recent efforts by Lucy Pearl, Jurrasic 5, Macy Gray,  and Amel Larrieux, and not try to stuff Morcheeba back into a moody  trip-hop shell that they have since shed.  By the way, Skye can teach a lot  of today's divas the deeper meaning of SOUL, arguably even moreso here than  on the prior albums!To Morcheeba, hopefully you'll pick up ten new fans  for every change-resistant one you'll lose, because I would love albums  such as this to overthrow the juvenile attitude of much popular culture  (i.e., for those of us who aren't into plastic images and profane  attitudes).
summary: Morcheeba puts a smile on their talent...and my face!

reviewText: Phil Collins might not get a lot of respect from older rock fans now because of the string of R&B; influenced hits but the fact is that he made some terrific pop music in addition to his work with Genesis and past work with jazz fusion band Brand X."Face Value" remains, for me, his best and most adventurous solo album--at turns commerical and pushing the boundaries ("In The Air Tonight" which has a strong influence evident from Peter Gabriel's third solo album from the composition itself to the production courtesy of the engineer of that album Hugh Padgham with the gated drum sound)it's a terrific album filled with honest, direct songwriting (so much so that I feel Gabriel used Collins album as a departure point when he made "So" 5 years later).Regardless, the big question here is whether or not the original standard CD or the newer gold CD issued from Audio Fidelity are the the ultimate edition. Let me be clear--the original CD mastered by Barry Diament sounds terrific--nice detail, clarity, dynamics, midrange and, considering that Diament was working from an analog copy of whatever the UK used as the master).Steve Hoffman who remastered this CD went back to the original master tapes for this edition (although it's not noted on the packaging because Audio Fidelity has had to use--particularly in the case of the Stevie Wonder remasters--safety masters or copies when the original master tapes were not available)has done a great job with this reissue. Will you hear a difference? That really depends on 1) where you're going to listen to this 2) your equipment and, ultimately, your ears. You like what you like. If you've found that the difference between between remasters that receive praise and the original CDs isn't that much of an improvement, you'll probably hear little or subtle differences. If you just like to crank these up in the car with the windows down, it's not likely you're going to hear a lot of difference. If you listen, on the other hand, with headphones or focus on little things like the warmth of the mastering, etc. you will notice a difference.I'd have to give the edge to Hoffman's master in a number of listening environments (my main system, in the car, on my ipod, etc.)as depth, clarity (due to improved A/D equipment)and warmth are all improved. Again, your mileage may vary so that's something to consider. I do wish that AF would use SACD as a format (I also understand why they don't--expense, the profit margin is thinner, less plants to press, a bit more complicated QC, etc.)but that's not part of this discussion really.I can recommend this--you'll hear improvements largely dependent on your ears and your listening environment so if you're satisfied with you hear on the regular CD and are immune to subtle differences, you may want to spend that money somewhere else. Nevertheless, this is a great sounding remaster but the choice is ultimately yours.
summary: Terrific sounding remaster BUT hearing the difference depends on your ears and listening environment

reviewText: ZZ Tops long slow climb to the top of the hard rock tree at the height of the MTV hair metal daze was almost unfair given that the band were quite a lot more vital than many of their fellow stars. Being born in the 70's and having a hard rocking pedigree that so many of the other bands that were around them didn't during the mid 80's means that it's unfair to find ZZ Top guilty by association.Yet their big bucks heyday did go a long way to forever imbedding their status as a novelty hard rock act totally obsessed with well endowed women wearing not much of anything on MTV and this best of is certainly guilty of pandering to their late 80's/early 90's phase. A quick look at the track listing proves that this is a veritable casual fans delight. Really, the casual hard rock fan or the casual Top fan can't really go wrong here in terms of picking up a slice of southern tinged hard rock Americana. The big radio hits: Gimme All Your Lovin, Sharp Dressed Man, Got Me Under Pressure and Legs are all here. Even lesser hits like Doubleback come alive when surrounded by the bearded ones choicest cuts. While some of the double entendre is a bit forced (Pearl Necklace) it's really not much worse than that of bands like AC/DC or early Skid Row (I'm thinking Big Guns here).A highway album for sure, this is an album that you can just put in and press play and let the deeply blues steeped toe tapping hard rock thump out of your speakers and wash over you. It should also be noted that some of the tunes here were remastered which is perhaps fair enough given tunes like La Grange reach all the way back to 1973 though the simpler production values of the 70's are actually perfectly suited to ZZ Tops working mans boogie rock. The liner notes sadly don't really add much apart from some trivia knowledge and the fairly tacky cover and booklet art is pretty cringeworthy.Those little quibbles aside this is probably a pretty darn useful album for anyone who has lived under a rock since these guys started out. The fact that the source album for each track is duly noted is a bonus, allowing the listener wanting to explore their reasonably extensive back catalogue a clue as to where to start based on what tunes they like most.A good career retrospective, whether the purists agree or not, and well worth your dollar.

reviewText: The third Fugee to release a solo album. I think that among all the Fugees, his the only one who kept the original Fugee style, which is cool. Oh no, don't think the song's are totally similar, Pras also has his "Ghetto Supastar" style! Anywayz, his style is terrific! The album starts by Pras showing how grateful he is to God with the open "Hallelujah" chorus done by a choir. This then leads into the rhymes, the beats and the rhythm of the streets. His debut single "Ghetto Supastar" starts off with a talking intro by that Ol' and a smooth-ballad chorus done by Mya. Pras' verses are tight as what! Ol' Dirty Bastard also throws in some amazing rhymes, an absolute "ghetto" track! Of course, Pras is not gonna give you an album without, gangsta rap style which proves on "Can't Stop The Shining" with Free and Canibus, not to mention Lenny Kravitz playing some hard rock guitar as a background to hard headed spat out rhymes. Throughout the album Pras mainly features the ReFugee Camp Allstars new comers like the amazing R&B duo, The Product G&B. He features them on most of his songs. His rap-ballads are tight, the one that stands out nicely is "What'Cha Wanna Do" and a nice and smooth "Get Your Groove On" If you didn't notice, Pras only used four samples, when as Wyclef and Lauryn used quite a bit for their albums. He used two songs written by The Bee Gees members. If you a type-a person who wants a party bumpin' then listen to tracks like "Wha' What Wha' What" some tight R&B, Hip-Hop and Rap party tune. I think Pras has done an excellent job for himself on this one, congratulations on such a good project is what peeps should tell 'em! Pras is da man, da Fugee and most importantly da GHETTO SUPASTAR!

reviewText: A landmark in popular music, incorporating so many styles of music into one very strange (and wonderful) brew indeed, from blues to jazz to pop, this album brims with energy, evocative melancholy at times, and a concluding streak of goofy good humor. The majority of the lyrics are from the fertile mind of poet Pete Brown, Jack Bruce's longtime collaborator, shot through with dazzling & haunting images -- "Dance the Night Away" is especially powerful & otherworldly -- but Martin Sharp's lyrics for "Tales of Brave Ulysses" are equally wonderful, bright & vivid as the tiles of a Mediterranean mosaic, conveying the mythic essence of The Hero's Journey on several levels at once. These songs have all the sweep & soaring drive of much of the progressive rock that was to emerge on the scene soon after, wrapped up compactly in the form of succinct pop songs. And for those who complain about Ginger Baker's vocals on "Blue Condition" -- his lugubrious delivery absolutely suits the tone & lyrics of this song; you couldn't improve on it! While the band strives for Big Things, they never fear to grin happily on occasion. All in all, an exceptional album from beginning to end. Highly recommended!

reviewText: This is the first album (CD) I have ever purchased, and it turned out to be a great album!  My father had a great collection of Billy Joel works through the 70's, 80's, and 90's.  But, for some reason he didn't have this album; I guess "The Stranger" over shadowed this album!I really have to thank Billy Joel because it was this album that really made me indulge into music.  He puts a lot of effort musically as well as lyrically, making all of his works unforgetable.  How can you forget, "Scenes at the Italian Restaurant" for an example.Now, this album "Turnstiles" is a classic work!  There is no question about that. The album has a good flow to it; all the songs come together well, one song doesn't over show the others.  Again the lyrics are awesome here, you can't get away with not learning new words with his complex lyrics.Many would call "Piano Man" his break through album, but personally his real master work "Turnstiles" is what gave Billy Joel worldwide attention and fame by setting the plateform for the "The Stranger."  Although "Piano Man" acquired more attention, his "Turnstilles" album performs better if you give it time.If you don't have this album, it's a must get.  Out of all Billy Joel works, it's among the few that stands up to "The Stranger."

reviewText: 1991's Dangerous includes many of Michael Jackson's under appreciated masterpieces. "Black or White" was a ubiquitous smash and certainly one of his greatest pop hits, but many other forgotten singles and album tracks rank right beside it. "Remember the Time" sounds like an updated "Rock with You" and, as such, is one of his greatest R&B efforts. The surprising "In the Closet," one of the most sensuous recordings of his career, features an addictive arrangement of tough, rhythmic verses and melodic choruses. One of Jackson's trademarks is the inclusion of a rock track on each album. "Give into Me," with its incredible electric guitar solo from Slash, is one of his best. "Will You Be There" is a powerful anthem that captures Michael at both his most vulnerable and his most triumphant. Though it includes a handful of less memorable tracks, Dangerous features many career highlights, ensuring its position as a classic album. 4 Stars.

reviewText: Before Eminem, there was Redman. Much like Eminem, Redman uses many analogies, metaphors, sick wordplay to tell graphic and often time humorus stories. Eventhough Redman was first, he's not quite as good as Eminem. Although Redman may have as much "rewind" material as Eminem, Redman never brings anything special or different to the table. That's where this album falls just a little bit flat. Sure, the songs are great and funny but we've already been there and done that. "Soopaman Lova", "Smash Somethin", "Let's Get Dirty", and "Enjoy the Ride" are all great songs that compare well to previous Redman efforts. I just wish we could get more into the mind of Redman and avoid the usual sex/drugs/violence/party aspects for a few tracks. Still a very enjoyable CD that is worth your money, however.

reviewText: This was one of my first techno CDs and it still remains one of my favorites.  This CD, while not as mellow as Experience (another great CD), is much more danceable then their overrated "Fat of the Land."  This is not a perfect album; a couple of tracks like 7, for example, may be  a bit on the annoying side. Still, there is so much on this CD that you can  easily forgive a few small missteps.  In my opinion, songs like Voodoo  People, Poison, No good are classics. Prodigy proves here that they are  very good at blending hard rock with fast and exciting dance rythms. A must  for any electronica fan or anyone who is at least remotely interested in  this kind of music.

reviewText: OK, at first I was skeptical and I thought that FSF would never be any good without Carraba. I deserved a swift kick in my corduroy trousers. "How To Start A Fire" takes the talent of FSF to a whole new level and makes for probably the best album of 2003 and it's only April. Along with the new vocals of Jason Gleason comes new songwritng which means deeper lyrics and since the band has been together as is for two years, they sound much tighter. Lyrically, there is no comparison between "The Moon Is Down" and "How to Start a Fire" the latter seems to come off as more artsy and metaphorical,which is awesome. The albums are to be viewed as two separate entities, each great for different reasons. My favorite tracks on the record seem to be all of the even numbers. "The Sound", "Pride War", "Insincerity...", and "Against My Better Judgement" are four songs can't seem to stop listening to. The rest of the album is also stellar. I find Gleason's vocals more polished and less nasally than Carraba's and Gleason seems to get away with screaming but not quite screaming, just a raising of his voice that is extremely cool. If you haven't bought this album, I don't know what could possibly stop you. You will listen to it for years. Maybe even thousands of years.

reviewText: I missed the boat on the first couple of White Stripes CDs and was fully prepared to hate them when I bought ELEPHANT--talk about a boatload of hype being forced down down your throat by Rolling Stone and every other out-of-touch music rag--but after four straight days of listening to ELEPHANT at top volume, I am here to say that the White Stripes have got it going on."Seven Nation Army" is getting the airplay, but the whole album rocks. Kind of like Sweet meets Smashing Pumpkins, with Guns & Roses and the Spiders from Mars playing backup. I mean, they ROCK. There is a lot mure THUMP! to the White Stripes than your typical 21st century band; they appreciate big guitars and are a thousand times more creative than anyone else going right now.As far as I'm concerned "Girl, You Have No Faith In Medicine" is thE Rock song of 2003, an absolute ass-kicker with some of the best singing I've heard by a guy on a Rock record since Kurt Cobain fled the scene. Jack White also plays guitar like Mick Ronson, and you can't beat that.The shortcoming of the White Stripes, as with a million other bands, is that they can't be hard and soft on the same LP. The lighter stuff here--and there isn't much--sounds forced, contrived. If the Stones, Beatles, Zep, Who, and other classic Rockers can point to one thing that sets them above most of the other bands that have attempted the crown since then, it is that they could play both sides of the coin--the Stones had "Midnight Rambler" and "Angie," the Who had "Love Ain't For Keeping" on the same LP as "Won't Get Fooled Again."Jack White comes really close on "I Want to Be The Boy...", and Meg White attempts some kind of subtlety on "In the Cold, Cold Night," but it really just sounds like one of those blank-generation Goth things Concrete Blonde used to do. There comes a point when a singer needs to put across something deeper; when the White Stripes get to that point they will be a truly great band. I suppose the secret may be to keep Meg behind the drum kit while Jack stretches his vocal chops.
