reviewText: Jay-Z released his 1st (and best) album in 1996, two years after the classic "Ready To Die" by The Notorious B.I.G.  "Reasonable Doubt" is one of my favorite rap albums and it is filled with 14 outstanding tracks (and 1 bonus track).  This album is Jay-Z before he became commercial (although he still had skills later on, he just became more of an image).  With "Reasonable Doubt", Jay-Z released a classic album filled with exceptional rhymes and stories.  This was when he was a hustler from the streets who rapped about what he knew - and did it very well.  You can tell how hungry we was at this time and his detailed experiences on the streets are great due to his brutal honesty and some very creative rhymes.  So before you trash Jay-Z's legacy due to some of his later albums, go back and listen to this because it alone, cements his legacy as one of the best MC's.1. Can't Knock The Hustle - Great song to start off the album featuring Mary J. Blige. Great beat, great hook, and as usual, Jay-Z lays out some great lyrics and his flow on this song is as good as it gets. "Through my peripheral I see you scheming. Stop dreaming, I leave your body steaming." 10/102. Politics as Usual - I don't know what it is but I really like this beat. It's really simple but it compliments Jay's especially tight rhymes in this song. This song really shows Jay-Z cocky, cool, and laid-back rhymer that he is. "You ain't seen money in your life, when it comes to this cheese y'all like Three Blind Mice." 10/103. Brooklyn's Finest - Classic song.  My favorite song on the album. It's great to hear these two amazing MC's together and since Biggie is my favorite rapper, I especially like it.  Both of them tear up their verses and it's great. "You're holding more drugs than a pharmacy, you ain't harmin me. So pardon me, pass the safe, before I blaze the place." 10/104. Dead Presidents II - Great song with the Nas sample. Jay makes it into a really hot song with some great lyrics. Just as good as Part I, maybe better. "Crime Family, well connected Jay-Z and you fake thugs is Unplugged like MTV." 10/105. Feelin' It - Nice feel good track with a slow and laid back beat. Jay's lyrics are tight as usual and he's got some standout rhymes in here that keeps this album moving along. "Even if it ain't sunny hey I ain't complaining. I'm in the rain doing a buck forty hydroplaning." 9/106. D'Evils - 2nd best song on this album in my opinion.  Jay-Z made a classic right here that doesn't really seem to get it's respect. It's often overlooked.  It's basically about having to be willing to anything to get what you want and it's also about how friends can change when money and success enter the picture. "And even if Jehova Witness bet he'll never testify." 10/107. 22 Two's - Really nice track in which Jay-Z lays out a freestyle in which he says either two, to, or too 22 times throughout the 1st verse. Simple concept but he manages to lace some very creative rhymes in the midst of his count. "No question, Jay got too many answers. I been around this block, too many times. Rocked, too many rhymes; Cocked too many nines." 10/108. Can I Live - Pretty decent song with a good beat and some nice rhymes. Not really a standout track but it's still a great song and Jay sounds hungry in his rhymes. "Dreams of getting cheese. It gets te-di-ous. So I keep one eye open like CBS." 8/109. Ain't No N**** - Probably the weakest of the 14 original tracks.  Jay's verses are pretty good but not outstanding.  Foxy Brown is featured but once she starts to spit, you really wish she wasn't. The beat isn't really that great and overall, it's not up to par with the rest of the album. 6/1010. Friend or Foe - Outstanding song. This song really shows Jay-Z the hustler step out and make himself known. The lyrics are blazing but the song is too short. Still, a great song. "Your draw better be Picasso, you know the best. Cause if this is not so, ah, God bless." 10/1011. Coming Of Age - Really tight song that introduces Jay's supposed successor and protege Memphis Bleek. Bleek is pretty nice on here but he's never managed to really make a standout solo album. Still, good song about a hustler and a kid who wants to make it big as well. "I'm out here serving, disturbing the peace but life could be better like my man reclined in plush leather seats." 9/1012. Cashmere Thoughts - A pretty good song but it doesn't have a very good beat. Jay's got some good rhymes but not a standout, just a pretty good song. "The proper ettiquette when I drop the subject verb, then the predicate." 7/1013. Bring It On - Good song featuring Jay's mentor Big Jaz. Good beat, good lyrics, all you can ask for in a good song. "Liason for days on in. Money make the world go around so I made songs to spin." 9/1014. Regrets - Great song to end the album (not including the bonus track).  Jay-Z tells about having to live with regrets in order to live the life he's lived and he tells his story over a great, light beat and with some very nice, slow lyrics. "I miss him, as long as I'm living he's living through memories. He's there to kill all my suicidal tendencies. In heaven looking over me, or in hell, keepin it cozy." 10/1015. Can I Live II - I hate to include this as a song on this album but if I were to, it would definately be the worst. There's not much to say.  It has a pretty weak beat and some disappointing lyrics from Jay and Bleek. Just unnecessary. 5/10Overall, a classic album by Jay-Z and this is the best East Coast album in my opinion following the work of the The Notorious B.I.G.

reviewText: Out of the albums I own buy Madonna: Like a Prayer,Erotica,Bedtime Stories,Ray of Light, and Music, this is the one I could get in to the most(this is not to say those other albums are bad, but this is the one I come back to the most). I love the oh-so catchy "Secret", such a good song, the sassy "Human Nature", The lush "Take a Bow", the soul-baring "Inside Me", the goovy "Survival", the carefree "Don't Stop", and the surreal Bjork penned title track. It makes for a diverse, yet cohesive album that saw Madonna stretching in to new musical territory, in this case soul music, which she has, sadly, never truly revisited, it was a great fit for her.This is a lot different then her other albums, its more on the soulful side of things then her previous releases, and the releases after, it is very smooth and groovish, as well as very sensual, without being explicit like erotica, it is the beats and melodies, not the words that create the mood. This music is good, and the language isn't too explicit except on "Human Nature", but it is put to good use.This may not have been the era Madonna is most remembered for, but her it both her most refined effort, and gives up glimpses of Madonna could have blossomed in to if she dropped the need-to-shock mentality and wouldn't have converted to Kaballah and went whole sell in to electro-pop.God Bless ~Amy

reviewText: Jackson Browne's self-titled debut, along with FOR EVERYMAN, LATE FOR THE SKY, THE PRETENDER, and RUNNIN' ON EMPTY, is one of his best. The songs ask questions about hard-to-ponder subjects, and really make the listener think. This album is a must-own for anyone who loves California rock, Southern rock, or Midwestern rock, and considering that Browne advocates sanctions on Indonesia in retaliation for that country's recent trumped-up drug-smuggling conviction of a young Australian tourist, as well as more funding for community policing, this album is also an essential purchase for your conscience.

reviewText: The tenor saxophone battle has a long and distinguished heritage in jazz.  But it took leader Dizzy Gillespie to enable Sonny Rollins and Sonny Stitt to be able to have some fun.  And for all the great saxophone blowing here, there's some phenomenal trumpet wailing too.  The sound quality on this album is amazing.  Every single song on this album make this album a must have.  Ray Bryant's solo on After Hours is so bluesy and so smooth it is hard to touch.  Having both Sonny Stitt AND Sonny Rollins on the same session is a good enough reason to buy this album and even though their techniques are both of modern jazz persuasion, their approaches can be quite dissimilar.  And both symbolize two differing perspectives in current jazz improvisation.  On the Sonny Side of the Street is just such a sweet little piece and you may be thinking What the heck is Dizzy doing singing? Don't worry he actually has a pretty good voice.  But anyways, even if you are not familiar with any of these artists, but are into jazz this is a must have album.
summary: A Must Have for any Jazz Enthusiast

reviewText: PORCUPINE TREE has never failed to fully satisfy the pickiest rock listener, and DEADWING surpases even the highest of expectations.  Easily the best CD of 2005, this one rocks with great authority and purpose.  STEVEN WILSON proves yet again that his musical instincts are dead on.  The guy oozes talent.  He and his equallly talented bandmates have made a record rife with great riffs, melodic hooks, and long interludes of sonic splendor.  The song ARRIVING SOMEWHERE BUT NOT HERE is an absolute epic that induces breathlessness.  Every track on the record bristles with a ferocious, desperate electric current that shakes the spine.  PORCUPINE TREE is simply the best rock band you've never heard of, and if you haven't, you're really missing out.  Awesome disc.

reviewText: I love the fact that there are so many 5 star reviews for this album; one guy compares this to Jackson Browne, and he is really onto what they were after when they created this.  This is the first time a metal band expanded their pallette to really include an adult contemporary audience in their net.  This is also probably the only band talented enough to be able to.  So you not only have Browne, but also Springsteen ("Desert Plains"), Billy Joel, and a good helping of the Stones.  A true, passionate, and intelligent work; this is one of the most original albums I've ever heard.

reviewText: Tender Lover came out in July of 1989 and you can see up to this day I still blow the dust off of it and let it flow all threw the house. I have to say that I have been a Kenneth Babyface Edmunds fan since he was just a guitar player for the Delle and I have watch him develope into one of todays hottest male vocalist.  This is one of the best CD's ever recorded from start to finish this will blow you away. reviewText: Please stop calling this the best CD ever. You have got to be kidding yourself. I admit a few songs had potential, like Around the Fur and Be Quiet And Drive, but they just wasted them. My Own Summer steals the riff from Metallica's The Outlaw Torn and most of the other songs sound like they used the first riff that popped in their head and used it for the whole song. That's too bad, since everyone in the band is talented, as shown in the fury and hooks of Adrenaline (Before Chino ruined his voice by shouting so much) and the beautiful music of White Pony. Try those out if you like, but be quiet and drive (far away from this CD).

reviewText: How to best describe the music of Fleet Foxes music? I guess this is really no easy task . On the one hand, you could say that the music is reminiscent of a whole lot of other artists and that the band uses familiar elements from known genres. On the other hand I can not think of anyone who is really reminiscent of Fleet Foxes .You might start by saying that it is modern folk music with extensive use of 1960s pop and psychedelic elements. Artists like Paul Simon, The Beach Boys, Graham Nash and maybe Crowded House might be names that could come to mind while listening to Fleet Foxes’ second album ” Helplessness Blues”.The music is melodious, with fine vocal harmonies and actually quite catchy. When I first listened through the album, I was really impressed and had a feeling of just having "discovered" a great band. Unfortunately this feeling left me after a second listening, when several tracks seemed a bit unattractive and in some cases somewhat pompous.It can not be denied that the group has produced a great sounding album and a handful of songs undoubtedly have durability. These could include Montezuma , Sim Sala Bim , Battery Kinzie and Lorelai .Whether Fleet Foxes is really a new "big" band I doubt, on the other hand I dare not totally exclude this.

reviewText: So here's the thing.  I am not a Joss Stone fan.  I do not own any album by her, and have only listened to her music briefly in the past.  I heard "Introducing" today, and was blown out of the water.  Her previous albums just did not encompass the sheer power and majesty of this girl's pipes.  The music that supports this amazing instrument is quite suited to it, and is phenomenal on it's own.  Joss has also acquired a nice collection of supporting starts, including Common and Lauryn Hill (who's voice is a welcome one...does this herald future Lauryn Hill material?  Here's hoping.)  Her lead single from this album, "Tell Me 'Bout It" is an upbeat funky number with plenty of sass and style.  "Music", with Lauryn Hill, is a slowed-down groove with a great message about Joss herself, and is a fantastic number to sit back and relax to.I could go into more detail, but what's the point?  Just buy it.

reviewText: Little Feat had been rolling along quite well by 1973. A promising debut (Little Feat) and a very even and fantastic record later (Sailin' Shoes), they hit the mainstream in a big way with their 3rd album, 1973's Dixie Chicken. When Roy Estrada left the band, Lowell George and company decided to revamp the lineup. With Kenny Gradney replacing Roy on bass and the addition of Paul Barrere on guitar & Sam Clayton on percussion, Lowell became infatued with New Orleans style R&B; and the band sounded more laid-back, but at the same time, very heavy-hitting. Gone are the weird psychedelic experiments of the previous records, and in it's place are funky laid-back rock songs with terrific hooks.Dixie Chicken still has the lyrical oddities and eccentricities of the earlier releases, but in their wake is a great collection of tunes, arguably the best the band has ever written. The songs are easy to remember, but at the same time, they are highly sophisticated and has some very deep interplay between all the band members. The title track alone is one of the highlights of the band's career, a slow funky jam with terrific slide playing by George. Other standouts include the energetic Two Trains, the creepy Kiss It Off, and one of my favorites, Juliette, a fusion of jazz, rockabilly, and R&B; that shows how diverse the band really was.Lowell doesn't get all the spotlight, of course. Bill Payne has really stepped up on this album and has delivered the Stones swagger of Walkin' All Night. Also, guest writer Fred Tackett gave the band Fool Yourself, one of the best songs the Eagles never wrote (The Eagles only wish they could sound this good). A fantastic Allen Toussaint cover rounds out the album too, All Your Way Down, with some very cool and relaxed playing, but still played with menace and foreboding.Little Feat, along with many jam bands of that era, tried to top this album, but this is the cream of the crop. This is the first perfect Little Feat album, and, unfortuantly, it would only go downhill from here. But this album is perfect from beginning to end. Buy if you love good rock and roll.

reviewText: It's ridiculous how many bands nowadays blatantly rip off the Cars without anyone calling them on their crap.  "Stacy's Mom," anyone?  Weezer or Hot Hot Heat, perhaps?The reason for all of this idolatry is, of course, because the Cars' debut album is still one of the freshest and most vital pop albums ever.  The record was released in 1978, and it never ceases to amaze me with just how timelessly perfect it still sounds.With simple, catchy, and infinitely memorable songs, the Cars' debut is the official soundtrack to a good time.  Easily one of the 70s' best.  "Just What I Needed" is among my top five favorite pop songs ever.

So over all this is an ok cd, but people who are looking for the same heavy and rough sounding taproot, don't bother with this cd.  It's like a counting crows album compared to gift.

reviewText: No, I'm not labeling this as bubblegum pop-this album is far from it!!  I just recently got into Meteora as a result of liking Linkin Park's current singles.  I love how LP fuses mellow rap with hard rock!  Finally, something original in new music!!  I hate most rap, but with Linkin Park, you can actually understand what they're saying.  They also rap and sing about  problems that the average person can relate to-just listen to "Numb" and "Hit The Foor"!  It's more than just hoes, bling-bling, drugs, and 24-inch rims!  But at the same time the hard rock part isn't about blood, guts, and suicide either.  Unintelligible scream fests are also kept to a minimum here as well.  Plus, unlike other major hard rock acts, Linkin Park doesn't need to say F*** 30 times per song to get their point across!  All in all, an excellent alternative rock album with VARIETY-which is something I don't find too often with new albums!  I don't even need to skip over tracks!  Give it a try!  I'm a major Britney and 'N Sync fan, and this album even made ME take a second glance!  No, I'm not some teenybopper trying to fit in with the cool crowd at the local Hot Topic store.  I couldn't care less what the latest "goth" fashion is.  I'm a twenty-year old college student with no one that I care to impress!  I also don't feel the need to attach a music genre label to myself, such as the term "punk".  Sorry for dragging on like this, but I am so sick and tired of close minded people! By that, I mean people who think I am only entitled to listen to pop music just because I have the Backstreet Boys in my CD collection!  I figure no one is in the same mood all the time, so why listen to only one type of music?

reviewText: Jill Sobule is a smart and witty songwriter who keeps gaining maturity with each progressive CD. "Pink Pill" is a more enjoyable recording thanHappy Town, in that the songs seem less dark and more peppy. The character songs are still the ringers here, from the body maniac with low self-image in "Lucy At The Gym" who discovers that everyone in heaven is perfect to "Mary Kay," about Mary Kay Letourneau, the teacher who had sex with a 13-year-old student.I have two favorites on "Pink Pearl," and they are the wonderfully sad tale of unrequited love in "Mexican Wrestler" and the darkly funny "Heroes." In the later, Jill bemoans the fact that all the folks she looked up to creatively were train-wrecks."William Faulkner, drunk and depressed.Dorothy Parker, mean, drunk and depressed,And that guy in Seven Years in Tibet turned out to be a Nazi.The founding fathers all had slaves.The explorers slaughtered the braves.The Old Testament God can be so petty."All set on top of a great shuffle with a goofy electric piano solo. The only artists who reach these kinds of musical epiphanies would be Aimee Mann (a lot of "Pink Pearl" is reminiscent of Mann's "Bachelor No. 2") and the late Warren Zevon, who Jill often toured with. While I still rate hersecond albumand "Underdog Victorious" as her better albums, there is still plenty to enjoy on "Pink Pearl."
summary: I can crack your ribs but I can't break your heart

reviewText: There sure was a lot of hoopla when this album dropped in 1996. New Edition had reunited after a near decades absense from the record racks. During the time they'd been absent of course Bobby Brown,Johnny Bill and the spinoff group Bell Biv Devoe had all been hugely successful at mining the R&B sound of the era and making the groove work for them on every level. The interesting part is that this is a comeback album that finds the group in a state of transition. It was deeper than any personal thing. During 1996 the sound of new jack swing to which they'd belonged for some time was starting to be shunted aside as a new type of hip-hop based R&B was slowly worming it's way into the musical subconcious of the people. This new type of music was slower,funkier and more organically fasioned than the music pioneered by Teddy Riley and LA Reid half a decade earlier. The one place where this album is inpeccable and nearly flawless is in the vocal department. Brown and Gill trade off vocal licks in the classic Motown/Chicago soul tradtion and the combintion of vulnerability,swagger and sexuallity comes off on every cut. Musically it's another matter. Bringing in the talents of Jam & Lewis,Gerald LeVert,the man now known as Diddy (Sean Puffy Combs then) and the relatively knew Jermaine Dupri along with themselves we're already dealing with four very individual and powerful production teams here. James Brown funk samples abound of course there is of course a strong pimping/mack daddy orientation to the lyrics and the music and with proper care "Oh Yeah,It Feels So Good","Tighten It Up","Hear Me Out" and the like could've been outright ingenious. The trouble is the actually songwriting of those three tunes and most of what else is here is rather bland and pressed out for the most part:melodically,harmonically and rhythmically the songs tend to have all too similar a structure-to the point where they start to sound kind of like remixes by the time you get halfway through. The interesting part is that also because of the heavy soul stew of the producers,the tapestry of vocals and the sound just mentioned this actually is one of the New Edition records that comes close to being a genuine album as opposed to an album stringing together singles. The two strongest tunes are "Hit Me Off",a darkly sexual funk groove with some of the best vocal arrangements on the album and the fact that you also get several of those on this one song adds to the sensual excitment. The closing Jam/Lewis produced title epic title track the group use a strong double meaning lyric that could easily be romantic but also reflects the group's earlier disbanding and reunion. The nice darkness and light style of the gospelish outro adds a certain uncertainty as well. New Edition were even at this point in the throws of change and while this album is not all it might've been it's more than an decent comeback.

reviewText: An album of Musically competant, arguably highly skilled , rock musicians, produced a rather less than stellar laststudio album in the this work.As Roger glover admits, they recorded enough for an album, 7 songs, with only oneouttake "Painted Horse". The Booklet is great as a narrative of the album. The Notable elements are The First DayJam is a jam with Ritchie on Bass guitar. One odd legacy of the album is when Gillan and an engineer ( Birch) werepunching some wood, Gillan winds up damaging a hand and at the hospital the reset left Gillan without a knuckle onhis small finger. Also Super Trouper is supposedly about Ritchie.The early part of the booklet makes it sound likethe recording of WOMAN FROM TOKYO was the only song recorded at a session, however, the latter part, it sounds likeGlover is saying that the material other than WOMAN FROM TOKYO was vetoed by Ritchie.So, if this is correct, whatmaterial was lost ?Prior to finding this album recently I was not aware of the music except for WOMAN FROM TOKYO which was agreat track on DEEPEST PURPLE.Tracks 8 and 9 have the remix of WOMAN FROM TOKYO( done by Glover, which sounds greatsince he has the start and full end of tracks on his mixes), and the alternative Bridge ( group 9 ).Tracks 1-7 havethe remix and remaster  which work great. Track 10 is an independent track. Track 11 is a Remix of OUR LADY .Track12, has Rat Bat Blue writing session. Track 13 has the Rat Bat Blue remix. And Track 14 has the Remix.Lyrically Ilike Mary Long and knew the content before I heard the explanation, it is so obvious to anyone with a particularbackground who it might be. Overall though, the stand out track in my view is WOMAN FROM TOKYO. The rest of thealbum seems less like a coherant band than previous albums and the material is not a continuation of previous albums, but more like a precursor to Ritchie's later works.Whilst it is annoying that the fights between ( it seems ) 2 significant band members kept things fromworking well within the style of the Mach 2 music, it is still an album that has been done well. Even with thedivergant tones of some songs, this album is piecemeal to some degree, but at least it shows all the work in studioat this stage. Maybe Glover will release that Revox Material.

reviewText: ...And I'm even more stunned by the volume of rave reviews for this mess. I hate this album, a LOT. It's incredibly boring, and instrumentally, a lot of it sounds like something I'd hear on an awful smooth-jazz or light-rock radio station. I have always favored Kate's upbeat songs, but that doesn't mean I hate this album because it's quiet. I like a lot of quiet music. But there's a fine line between pretty-quiet and boring-quiet. Aerial doesn't venture anywhere near that line...it is so dull and listless, there's no passion to be found on this two-disc set. Finally a Tori comparison that's warranted: both women have apparently given up on making interesting and passionate music, and sound these days as if their hearts just aren't in it.  And aside from the music, some of the lyrics even strike me as being really ridiculous.  I'm not usually one to dwell on lyrics (and truthfully, I wouldn't in this case either if I loved the music), but songs like Pi just make me roll my eyes.  If I wanted to listen to someone singing numbers, I would watch Sesame Street...at least THEY do it with enthusiasm.  ;-)After two days, I threw away my copy of Aerial. I'm sure I could have sold it, but I was feeling really disgusted at the time.Unlike some reviewers, I'm not out to attack people who don't share my opinion. You may love this album. Apparently, many people already do. But if you haven't bought Aerial yet, I discourage you from assuming that you'll love it just because it's getting great reviews.  Aerial is NOT for everyone, and I obviously regret buying it.

reviewText: This is one of those things you catch wind about and pick up at the store out of curiosity, wondering what it's going to contain.  You're almost sure to find something special about this one, though.  The first time i listened was probably a rainy day, and it's peaceful quiet is soothing.  Yet when looking at the lyrics, we see that Nick Drake was anything but peaceful and happy.  Still, he somehow managed to take all of his inner turmoil and create something absolutely magnificent and unique, which is one of the crazy things about genius.The guitar playing is reminiscent of classical runs, like a folk Mozart combination.  Drake's voice is light and unpretentious; quiet and naked.  The album's stripped down recording only adds to it's ambience, because you get to see the songs as they really are, a theory i dearly wish other artists would try.  There's nothing about this album that lies, it is only a man and his songs, and it can only be that.  Don't worry about classification, or about what music you already like, because this album will strike you the first time you hear it.  It's music that has no limit.

reviewText: Robin Thicke is the son of Alan Thicke (Canadian actor and singer) and Gloria Loring (American actress and singer). His musical album here is quite a variation of music and styles. He could be rapping in one song and singing in another with friends like Faith Evans, Lil Wayne, and Pharell to accompany him.I have to say that the album is unusual in selection of songs. Each song is unique and different from another which is fine. But I found the musical compilation to be too wide varied for my taste. I enjoy the smooth rhythm and blues style over the rapping songs anyway. I think Robin Thicke still needs to find his voice and style while he is very talented and this compilation is a good example of it. In my opinion, he still has more to go in evolving his styles and tastes.I do look forward to more mature Robin Thicke perhaps maybe including his parents to accompany him in the future. I do see plenty of promise in his talents.

reviewText: I was already an Eagles fan when The Long Run came out in '79, and I have both the CD and vinyl copies of the record.  "Heartache Tonight", which shot to #1 almost immediately, was the big hit from this album.  At that time, the Eagles were coming off their diamond(10-times platinum) Hotel California, a record they've never been able to top despite reuniting a few years ago after a long hiatus.  This record's definitely not Hotel California.  The Long Run is more guitar-driven; there's a keyboard on only six of the 10 tracks, and it is dominated by Joe Walsh, Don Felder, and even Glenn Frey on lead guitar.  Still, who cares?  The Eagles started out as a guitar-driven band, and The Long Run has a lot of solid guitar work."Heartache Tonight", with Glenn Frey's almost screaming lead vocals, is a boogie-rocker with an undercurrent of doom:  "Somebody's gonna hurt someone/Before the night is through...There's gonna be a Heartache Tonight".  An interesting bit of trivia:  one of Don Henley and Glenn Frey's co-writers on the song was Bob Seger, a Detroit buddy of Glenn's who is himself a legendary rocker.  The title cut "The Long Run" talks about "going the distance" with a romance and surviving tough times:  "We're scared, we ain't shakin'/We plan to bend, but we ain't breakin'", Don Henley sings.  Joe's power ballad "In The City" is self-explanatory:  "Somewhere out on the horizon far away from the neon lights/I know there must be something better/'Cause I can't stay another night/In the city".  "Teenage Jail", also sung by Glenn, could be a metaphor for the high school experience:  "Stare at the window, you can't make the time go/You don't even know why you're here/Wait for the weekend to go off the deep end".  "Those Shoes" could be the story of a vulnerable runaway trying to survive life on the street:  "Tell us what you gonna do tonight, momma/There must be someplace you can go/In the middle of the the tall drinks and the drama there must be someone you know."  "King of Hollywood" tells about a powerful, greedy Hollywood mogul who is described in very unsavory terms:  "Just another power junkie/Just another silk-scarf monkey/You'd know it if you saw his stuff/The man just isn't big enough".  The R&B-laced; "The Disco Strangler" and the frat-house rocker "The Greeks Don't Want No Freaks", both sung by Don Henley, are throwaway rockers.I thought The Long Run was skimpy on the ballads; only two songs on here are really slow.  Still, both of them are great.  Tim Schmit, who replaced Randy Meisner, contributed the classic romantic ballad "I Can't Tell You Why", which was a Top 10 hit:  "Every time I try to walk away/Somethin' makes me turn around and stay/I can't tell you why."  The closing song "The Sad Cafe" is the story of raised hopes and dashed dreams; as Don Henley sings, "We thought we could change this world with words like Love and Freedom/We were part of the lonely crowd inside the Sad Cafe."  I've listened to the record repeatedly, and I find those lines to be overblown and tired.  However, David Sanborn's saxophone playing and Don Felder's guitar, along with Don Henley's soulful lead vocals, more than compensate for the aforementioned cliche-ridden lyrics.The Long Run would be the "last hurrah" for the Eagles, at least for a while.  Though their breakup wouldn't become official until Don Henley and Glenn Frey released solo records in '82, the Eagles were on the decline as a group by the early '80s.  Thankfully, they've reunited, and their records are once again popular.  Check out The Long Run.  Hotel California it isn't; the Eagles haven't yet surpassed that one.  Still, The Long Run is a solid collection of songs from this legendary band.

reviewText: Whitesnake's self-titled album, was great when it came out in 1987, but it has sled a little since.  The bluesy Whitesnake had become part of the hair rock scene in 1987.  David Coverdale, Aynsley Dunbar, John Sykes, Neil Murray and Adrian Vandenberg (who had a hit in '82 "Burnin' Heart").  Their 9th studio release broke this band like wildfire.  This album gave us, the rockers "Children Of The Night", "Crying In The Rain", tremendous track, the Zeppelin clone song "Still Of The Night",#79, still one of my favorites from these guys.  The melodic rockers in, "Give Me All Your Love", #48, and the ballads that got played to death "Is This Love", #1, and "Here I Go Again", #2.  They would release "Slip Of The Tongue", in 1989.

reviewText: It took a long time for me to warm up to Mary Fahl's debut album, 'The Other Side Of Time', and I was very disappointed with it at first but it's gradually growing on me. Her deep, resonating vocals are an acquired taste and not for everyone but if you listen to her singing with an open mind than you'll likely become more acceptable to appreciating the exquisite beauty of her impressive range and eclectic style. With my purchase of Sarah Brightman's 'Harem', I received a free promotional disc called 'New Faces Of Music' which consisted of 9 songs from various artists emerging into the vastly spreading classical crossover genre. I was thus introduced to Mary Fahl's unique sound with the contemporary pop song, "The Great Unknown", which fails to sum the whole of her diversity, nor the finesse of her God-given talent, but it's a nice slice of the pie, nonetheless. On the wonderful compilation mentioned before, Mary stood out the brightest with me; like the only star in a darkened sky. I was instantly taken with the gorgeous intensity of her soaring vocals, which made me yearn to hear more as she imprisoned me in her thick layers of richly felt passion.I immensely enjoy this now but the only reason I'm dropping a star is because I tend to skip tracks and listen to the same ones over and over again, forgetting about the others. I find myself mesmerized with the first 4 songs and, my absolute favorite, "Raging Child". "Going Home" is a lovely culmination of folk and classical while the haunting "Ben Aindi Habibi", which is about a woman desperately begging her beloved to stay with her has some hypnotic Hindu textures to it. "Want To" is another personal favorite of mine and its, imo, the most breathtaking song on the album.Mary Fahl shows a lot of promise here and I'm sure that this is only the beginning of greater things to come.

"Going Home" is a lovely culmination of folk and classical while the haunting "Ben Aindi Habibi", which is about a woman desperately begging her beloved to stay with her has some hypnotic Hindu textures to it. "Want To" is another personal favorite of mine and its, imo, the most breathtaking song on the album.Mary Fahl shows a lot of promise here and I'm sure that this is only the beginning of greater things to come.

reviewText: Massive Attack's third album Mezzanine is a hard album to describe to someone who has never heard it. It has a very dark nature to it that might be expected from an Industrial act but at the same time it can be calm and relaxing. I do not like to use labels on Electronica music but "Trip Hop" is an appropriate term for this record. The feel of the record is a lot like a trip. You can put some head phones on and let it take you to a different world. It has heavy hip hop beats and the male vocal tracks are on the verge of being hip hop. It has the dark and urban feel of DJ Shadow and the mellow and laidback feel of Portishead. It takes some time getting use to. At first, I thought it was average and then I thought it was brilliant but now I think it is just damn good. There are moments in this record that deserve a 5 star rating but the album all together can get repetitive and is not as amazing as songs like "Angle" and "Rising Son" and "Interia Creeps." It is well worth buying and after buying "Mezzanine" I will definitely check out Massive Attack's other albums.

reviewText: A very steady recording indeed by Traffic. On this release, both Steve Windwood and David Mason contribute some excellent songs. Pearly Queen, Don't Be Sad, Who Knows What Tomorrow May Bring, Feelin' Allright, Cryin' To Be Heard, and You Can Join In are all catchy focused numbers with some captivating solos which are not overly extended. In addition, the vocals stylings are very expressive in the case of both Windwood and Mason. They both bring out every possible tone in their voices.Overall, the effort is consistent if not quite spectacular as John Barleycorn or Low Spark Of Hi Heeled Boys. Vagabound Virgin does drag after a while and the last two songs(not including the extra tracks) are not as good as the others. None the less, the prime time material on this record makes it a worthy purchase.

reviewText: A Somali refugee turned rapper, K'naan's album TROUBADOUR has a fresh vibe with lyrics that set it apart from generic rap with its heavy focus on ego and promiscuous sexuality. K'Naan provides nuance and intelligence mixed with solid hooks that listen a bit like Kanye West with African R&B; influence. There is a hint (and just a hint) of Marley in the mix, but this is understated, and only really take precedence in "T.I.A.""Dreamer," a song that could become a bit over the top in a sort of DANGEROUS MINDS way, K'naan is careful to throw in lines like "It's ok to have fun," and that seems to be the theme throughout the album. Interspersed with songs about the struggles of the poor, Somali pirates, and pulling oneself up by the bootstraps, K'naan never looses his cheerfulness. Even the more stereotypical "I Come Prepared" with its references to Russian firearms is still pretty fun.Throwing around words as diverse as "Bar Mitzvah" and "Tummy Tucks" and "Soundclash" and "Ghandi," K'naan proves he's got an education--even if it wasn't a formal one--and knows how to use it to comic, descriptive, and even powerful affect. The anthem "Waving Flag" is a hopeful tribute to the struggles of the suppressed (regardless of nation). Almost sweet, K'naan shows a willingness to be vulnerabley poetic, something hard edged American rappers obsessed with their 9mm or junk, could certainly learn from. There's an easy artistry to K'naan's hooks that makes this album thoroughly engaging.A highly stylish and endearingly fun album, TROUBADOUR has a refreshing honesty to it, fantastic hooks, and a political message that doesn't feel preachy, even when it's America getting lit up."A lot of underground *****'s are rappin' about rappin' / I just want to tell you what's really crack-il-akin / Before the tears came down this is what happened."And he does, and makes it damn enjoyable in the process.4.5/5 Stars. A definite buy if you like your rappers on the observant, intelligent, and cheerful side.

reviewText: I tend not to get too emotionally affected by music, mostly because I usually ignore lyrics unless they're especially clever, and well, a lot of musicians don't try that hard. But it's difficult to pay attention to Hospice at all and not get hit by it. It figures that only a couple weeks after I wrote a "best of 2009" list which featured nothing that made a huge impact on me, I'd hear an album as gripping as anything in recent memory. The music itself is only part of the equation, and you can't talk about Hospice without mentioning its origins. From what I can tell it's more or less the true story of the singer falling in love with a terminal bone cancer patient at the hospital where he worked. You can probably guess how well that works out.Despite the simple honesty of the lyrics, they never really hit you over the head with the message, and it's easy to ignore the content if you just want to hear a nice mix of shoegazing post-rock and indie folkiness (why isn't this a more popular combination?), though if you do you're not giving it a fair chance to do everything it can. Some people probably wouldn't want to hear an album that would only depress the hell out of them, and that's fine. But it's one of the more powerful listening experiences I've had in a while.Despite the sorrow of the words and the sincerity with which they're sung, it wouldn't work if the music was bad, and fortunately it's not. There's a fair amount of time spent without much happening beyond ambient noise, and it's difficult to love every moment when it feels like you're being pulled out of the flow a bit. There's a push and pull with the general sound as it goes between a strumming guitar and louder noise elements, and it could have gotten bogged down in its own seriousness. Luckily it's catchy enough in places to just be enjoyable to listen to, even while they're playing songs about abortion and knowing that someone you love is dying. I don't want to name individual tracks, because it really should be experienced as a full album, and it all runs together like one long piece of music. If you just want a taste though, it's okay to look up the music video for "Two". I'm definitely interested in seeing what this group does next now that this story has been told.

reviewText: Simon and Garfunkel were not just singers - they were incredibly talented poets who wrote words which touched your heart. Think of Shakespeare or Robert Frost put to music. You get not only the power of the words, but also the beauty fo the music.With Sounds of Silence, you get numerous classics - The Sounds of Silence, I Am a Rock, Kathy's Song for three. You also get a collection of less well known but just as intricate tunes - Leaves that are Green, Blessed, Somewhere they Can't Find Me, Anji, Richard Cory, A Most Peculiar Man, April Come She Will, We've got a Groovey Thing Goin'.Each song here has its own meaningful message. In I Am A Rock, they sing "I won't disturb the slumber of feelings that have died. If I never loved, I never would have cried." Quite a different view from 'Tis better to have loved and lost'!In The Sounds of Silence, they rail against people complacently accepting what they are told. "The people bowed and prayed to the neon god they made." Written back in 1965, the words are just as meaningful in modern times.Well recommended!

reviewText: "When your backs against the wall, you gotta bang your way out" (Lil Kim "Gon Delirious 2002). I'm willing to bet that this was the motivation that Ja Rule had in his head during the entire recording process of R.U.L.E. See Ja had become one of the leading rap stars in the game, with multi-platinum album after multi-platinum album and top ten single after top ten single. He was riding high an undeniable wave of success, and it seemed that his fire would never diminish. However his beef with another rapper, 50 Cent is what really hurt his carrer. 50 was the big dog on campus for a few months and ripped into Ja, much to the fans delight. However now that 50 has completely fallen off the face of the earth, its time for Ja to come out swinging.The album's first single "Wonderful" featuring R. Kelly & Ashanti is one of Rule's finest moments. A remix to "I Wonder" (which is no where to be found), the track is pop enough to dominate radio but street enough where Ja doesn't have to be dressed in a Grease varsity jacket a la "Mesmerized". And I never thought I would say this, but the inclusion of Ashanti was a wise decision. And with "New York, New York" featuring Fat Joe & Jadakiss starting to turn up on radio, its safe to say that he is going to have the urban radio market in the palm of his hand for quite some time.And while there are good things going on here, the album is still weak being that Ja doesn't register as much of a rapper. Lyrically he will not considered for the greatest of all time. Comments like "the streets damn near raised me" in "The INC" intro are what had Ja on the chopping block in the first place; he is much to soft to be claiming to be a gangsta. "Last of the Mohicans" has an infectious beat, but Ja fails to ride the beat, and the hook provided by Black Child just doesn't fit the record.It's tracks like "Get it Started" featuring the angelic voice of City High's Claudette Ortiz is where Ja feels most comfortable, and he sounds his best. So while he may not be the toughest dude in the game, thats ok he can bring it as the second coming of LL. It was that formula that made him all his cash anyway. Guest appearences by Llyod & Trick Daddy are worth a mention as well. I don't think Ja will have a hard time regaining the respect of his core audience, but its the street audience that is going to be his toughest challenge, and R.U.L.E. isn't going to be his homecoming welcome that he dreamed of. And my final thought, where is Charli Baltimore?

reviewText: LL Cool J is a legend in the game but sometimes legends don't realize when it's time to quit.  This kinda reminds me of Patrick Ewing's last few years in the NBA where he was looking absolutely horrible on the court; a very small shell of his former self.  Exit 13 is by far the worst LL Cool J album of all time.  Trust me it's a complete mess.  I did not think he could do worse than his last album (forgot the name of it) but he somehow outdoes himself.  I think he is trying too hard to be relevant again which is a shame.  LL Cool J should not be trying to make any club bangers.  His rapping style just sounds for lack of a better word "played"...it just doesn't sound right and really hasn't since the album "10" (which was his last good album).  The beats are terrible to say the least and the guests add nothing.  The Dream, 50 Cent, Fat Joe, Wyclef Jean among others cannot save this travesty.  I can't find a song that is even decent.  This album should be the nail in the coffin as far as LL's rap career goes.  Hopefully he can be a mentor or something like that and continue success in his acting career because he just doesn't cut it anymore.  LL Cool J one of the greatest of all time.

reviewText: I'm going to start off by saying that this is my first album from her. It's great and I imagine that it'd be hard for her other two albums to be better, especially Loose.But anyway...I'm now a big fan of Nelly Furtado because of this album. It shows her talent as a writer and also displays the truth, realism and magic that she is truly capable of.When she stepped on the scene in the early 2000s, I didn't really think much of her. In fact, her debut single, Like A Bird kinda made me want to smash the radio. However, there was something special about Turn Off The Light that caught my attention.Flash forward to 2003. Nelly drops her second album, Folklore and her first single from the album, Powerless (Say What You Want). While I liked the single, it didn't make me wanna go out and purchase the album, so I didn't. A year or two later, I was standing in line at Tops (before it got torn down and changed to Martin's) and her radio single, Try was on. One-Trick Pony is the start off track and is very "stand out-ish" with its oh-so-not-typical Hip-Hop beat. Explode is refreshing. reviewText: Still licking my wounds after the disappointment of Alanis' last studio outing (asides from Are You Still Mad?, Joining You & So Pure)which I felt struggled too much to differ from the uber-classic of Jagged Little Pill, the first chorus of this album's initial single Hands Clean, revitalised my interest in Alanis & hope that she would return to form.  Moreover, anytime you hear that an artist parts company with a manager or creative partner, you always think it means trouble.  Alanis' self-production of this opus made me fear for the worst.  Would she forgo her true sound?  Would she be able to reflect the verve that Glen Ballard helped her create?  This album has consolidated my hopes that Alanis would be better than before.  Phew!  From the opening confidence of 21 Things I Want In A Lover, the opening guitar rift gives me shivers, as does her multi-layered challenging 'Are you uninhibited in bed more than 3 times a week?', the vitriolicism is there, but with less anger than before. Classic song which will be mammoth, as it harks back to You Outha Know in its confidence & forth-right communication with Alanis' silent partner. The remainder of the album tend to veer towards a more relaxed Alanis.  No big rockers, but mid-tempo songs which allow Alanis to focus on her song-writing, & more importantly a decent chorus which doesn't contain more than 6000 syllables!!!! Another fave is Flinch, a tender ballad about letting go of a love & wondering if the painful feelings will be there later on (Soon I'll grow up, I won't even Flinch at your name).  Tragic, but personal one assumes. Alanis' voice on this album doesn't speak so much pain & rage which I felt the last 2 albums have (I've never indulged myself in her Tiffany-style music, & consider Jagged her first 'proper' album, as most do associate Control with Janet Jackson). However, the album does speak experience & sharing those feelings, or at least rationalising them out loud.  Precious Illusions & So Unsexy continue the difficulty of love theme with totall accessibility.  Remember as a youth lying on your bed identifying with the lyrics of Jagged Little Pill?  Well here's the next chapter which will help you on your merry way to further self-analysis.  Welcome back Alanis!!! This album will be a slow-burner & may take a bit of time to take off as audiences regain their faith in Alanis (although 8 million sales of the last album is by no means awful, but compared to the sales of Jagged you do note a stoop in audience interest I'm sorry to say).  21 Things & the remainder of the album should remind audiences who this gal is & moreover make them realise who exactly is at the wheel of her creative drive.  Glen who?????

reviewText: This 1991 debut, by an artist whose seeming anachrony hadn't hurt his chances of getting a record deal in the 90's, shows that good taste really had not disappeared entirely. This 11-song extravaganza will not blow out your speakers; rather, it is meant to be enjoyed for its subtlety and graceCohn's voice is suave and gruff all in the same motion, and his piano rings forth strongly. The big hit (and hands down, the greatest track) is "Walking in Memphis", a slow and evocative piece that makes adult contemporary more muscular. But it doesn't end there. "Silver Thunderbird" is a track reminiscent of early Springsteen in the exuberance of an era long past. Cohn sings with passion on a lot of these songs undoubtedly culled from his life's experiences."Strangers in a Car" relies only on Cohn's solid piano and story-telling ability to bring a chill to the spine. "Ghost Train" is a Gospel-like tune with great backup singing and organ music.The upbeat numbers don't detract from the mood, either. "Miles Away" and "Saving the Best For Last" offer less atmospherics and more commentary, with the latter giving one a heads up about the different characters you'd meet in New York City, if you found time to talk to a few; the former dealing with the funks we all get into sometimes. There's even a cover song, Willie Dixon's "29 Ways", with Cohn's pipe organ and unique back-up overdubs."Perfect Love" (with typical understated back-up singing by James Taylor) and "True Companion" are just flat-out wonderful love songs. The latter is especially touching, well-sung with a flourishing outro of an Irish bouzouki softly chanting out the finale.Absolutely masterful production tops off this great first effort by a musician who still hasn't equalled this original effort. But it is one to savor, nonetheless.

reviewText: "Even Now" spun off four of Barry's best singles in 1978:  "Can't Smile Without You", the title track, "Copacabana", and "Somewhere In The Night."  "Copa" is the best disco song ever by a non-disco act.  (This is  high praise in my book.  Everybody tried to get a disco hit in the late  '70's and the failures make a fantastic tape.)  It still sounds great  today, and how can anyone get tired of that intense storyline?  I've heard  "Can't Smile" and "Somewhere In The Night" on other  artist's records; the arrangements here run rings around them all.  Proof  of BM's skills as an arranger.  The moody title track is also a  highlight.Most of the remaining tracks are worth the purchase.  "Leavin' In The Morning" is catchy bubblegum-rock with coproducer  Ron Dante's fingerprints all over it.  "I Was A Fool (To Let You  Go)" is an early example of the jazzy pop Barry eventually came to  favor during much of the '90's.  There used to be some intrigue as to  whether "A Linda Song" was about our hero's real-life girlfriend  Linda Allen.  Or maybe not.  And there are echoes of the Stylistics in the  arrangement for "I Just Want To Be The One In Your Life," a  pretty love song.  On the down side, Barry's New Yawk accent is a bit too  noticeable on a couple of songs; his phrasing definitely improved over  time.  The bonus track "No Love For Jenny" is average, but better  by far than the album's worst song, "Losing Touch."  Overall, one  of Barry Manilow's best albums ever, and worth getting if you have any  interest in him at all.

reviewText: Tupac. A hard to describe person.... lemme try anyways.He was larger than life, unreal, yet the realest person alive.He was mysterious and complicated, but so straightforward a person who knew exactly where he stood.He was shy and sensitive, but at the same time, loud and angry.He knew exactly what he wanted and he worked towards it in the short time that he was on the planet. This is a testimony to his work, sadly only reflecting the songs that made the most money rather than the songs that truly deserve to be on here. Fortunately, though, most of the songs on here are amazing anyways.Disc One:1. Keep Ya Head Up- 10/10: A powerful track that enlightens you and makes you respect women and see them in a new light every time you hear it.2. 2 Of Amerikaz Most Wanted- 10/10: With Snoop, one of my favorite rappers back in the day, this makes for a great collaboration.3. Temptations- 7/10: Never was really a fan of this one.4. God Bless The Dead- 8/10: Kind of creepy. He's eulogizing Biggie, who died six months after him....5. Hail Mary- 10/10: This is one of my favorite Pac songs. The emotion on this song is unmatched, as he raps about evil, hatred, and corruption. The beat is pretty creepy.6. Me Against the World- 10/10: Another one of my favorite Pac songs. Powerful and delivering a great message to stay strong no matter what happens.7. How Do U Want It- 7/10: Never really was a big fan of this one.8. So Many Tears- 10/10: Great song.9. Unconditional Love- 8/10: Didn't really like this one.....10. Trapped- 8/10: From 2Pacalypse Now, this was Pac's first actual solo11. Life Goes On- 10/10: Awesome!12. Hit 'Em Up- 10/10: Before you get all upset that I gave this song a 10, read. Pac had every right to be mad at Biggie, even though I really don't thing Big shot him. Pac thought he did, and if you believe strongly that someone tried to murder you, I think you'd be pretty mad, too. This is one of my favorite diss tracks, but unlike Nas's Ether, it's not lyrically that great. I like it simply for the emotion and charisma Pac shows in the delivery. The outro, though, is uncalled for, and his attack on Mobb Deep for one of their members having Sickle Cell is downright disgusting. I didn't say the man didn't have flaws. The flaws just made him more human, which in turn made him more easy to relate to.Disc: 21. Troublesome 96'- 9/10- Pretty cool.2. Brenda's Got A Baby- 10/10: My favorite song on 2Pacalypse.3. I Ain't Mad at Cha - Danny Boy- 10/10: One of my favorite songs on All Eyez, this song really takes a risk with the piano, but it ends up helping the song rather than hurting it.4. I Get Around- 5/10: Arguably the worst Pac single ever released.5. Changes- 10/10. Great song!6. California Love (Original Version)- 10/10. So much better than the remix.7. Picture Me Rollin'- 8/10. Cool song.8. How Long Will They Mourn Me?- 10/10: 2 words: Nate Dogg.9. Toss It Up- 9/10. They only put this on here cuz it disses Dre.10. Dear Mama- 10/10: I'm a sucker for this one. I feel like hugging my mom every time I hear this song.11. All About U- 7/10. Just shouldn't be on here. Where's Snoop? Who the f**k is Top Dogg?12. To Live & Die In L.A.- 10/10: Kinda like the sequel to Cali Love.13. Heartz Of Men- 10/10: Lively, upbeat track.Pac is arguably the greatest MC of all time, simply for the emotion and charisma he puts in every single song. The new stuff that's coming out is bulls**t. Go buy a copy of this, and keep it with you. This is stuff that years and years later, when you feel down, you listen to Me Against the World and you get back to it. This is stuff that really gives you an insight into the troubled life and times of Tupac Amaru Shakur. This is stuff that you won't forget, no matter what kind of hip-hop fan you are. This is Tupac.Rest In Peace, 1971-1996. Tupac Amaru Shakur.

reviewText: After the immensely enjoyable "When I Look in Your Eyes" CD, I had high hopes and expectations for this highly-anticipated follow-up.  Krall owes a lot to her "When I Look..." CD, which converted more fans to jazz and Krall than any of her previous ones.  Imagine my surprise when I plopped "Look of Love" into my player.  Has Diana or her producers been listening to Lawrence Welk??!!  This CD lacks originality, purpose, or inspiration.  It seems the record company was trying to cash in on one of their biggest cash cows!!  I always thought Krall was one to play a bit too safe, but not THIS safe!!  She should also fire her publicist for making her pose in that hooker outfit on the CD cover---what an atrocious picture!!  I'm sorry to be getting down on Krall, but I'm sure as a fan, there are others like me who are very disappointed with this CD.  What about her piano-playing, they don't even get one song to show off here---it's all muzak strings thru and thru.Please, Diana, next time go back to your roots and come up with something more original----and please, put SOMETHING over that dress!!

reviewText: The only way to describe the new album by New Jersey stalwarts "Real Estate" is to echo the title of a sadly forgotten album by the Scottish band the Cosmic Rough Riders. Indeed their opus "Enjoy the Melodic Sunshine" has some similarities with "Atlas" since it often drew copious comparisons with bands like the Byrds, REM, Teenage Fanclub and the Jayhawks which are shared reference points for Real Estate. This album is essentially a blast of warm colour into a winter characterised by black sheets of rain. It is not a difficult listen by any standards, but there is real depth to be located in its grooves. It is safe to say that by the third listen "Atlas" will be a really good familiar old friend, one which you will turn to when you are confused for choice and you when you desire a reliable set of heartwarming shimmering pop rock headed up with with a capital "Q" for quality.Things start well on "Atlas" and get better. Indeed this reviewer has had to be dragged screaming from playing the first three tracks on repeat. The lovely opener "Had to Hear" jingles and jangles with Gene Clark like chords and a melody to kill for. It is splendidly bettered by the forlorn "Past Lives" destined to be the soundtrack as the dying embers of a summer barbecue fade into a dark night sky. Best of all is the joyous single "Talking Backwards" where the mix of Martin Courtney's bittersweet vocals and the flowing guitar lines of Matt Mondanile's pulsating guitar melodies reach a true synthesis. The joyful instrumental "April Song" reinforces this but the clinchers come later with the brilliant chiming chords of "Primitive" which is the best Norman Blake song he never wrote; concluding with a nice guitar workout to seal the deal. This blissed out state concludes with "Navigator" a melancholy ode to the way that time passes and defeats us.Ultimately you know what you get with this band. It may be that a "Real Estate plays Death Metal" album might be lurking in the depth of some unlikely recording vault, yet for now "Atlas" comfortably surpasses any of the bands previous two efforts and if their sin is "predictability" then their massive strength is great songwriting and the best ear for melody this side of Michael Stipe.

reviewText: In a lot of ways anticipating a Snoop album is like anticipating a KRS-One album. I mean, lyrically we have nothing to worry about. Both artists are absolutely brilliant with how they work the words. But for both artists I get a little anxious to see if the production will do even a hint of justice to their flow. I've never doubted Snoop's lyrical hustle. But the beats behind his rhymes are often an insult to his wordplay.And it kind of happens again with the Blue Carpet Treatment -- but not until a little after the mid-point of this album. At the jump, the Album is charged with smooth fire that is complimentary of Snoop's voice and flow. The moment "Think About it" rolls in my hopes went up and I thought this album was going to put all the others before it to sleep! "Crazy" has a crazy smooth beat. "Vato" has one of the most unique exotic electric sounds I've ever heard in a hip-hop song. And it seems like this energy keeps pushing onward and upward... until Tracks 14 thru 19, all of which --on a sliding scale of quality -- seemed to be below par. Well...actually, track 18 "Pump up your Pads" is an endearing track. I don't care for the beat, but lyrically -- as always -- Snoop can take any topic and make it sound good. Even if it's about young ball players.And then comes the save: "Imagine." This is by far the most memorable track on the whole album. Unlike most hip-hop songs where it takes a few listens before the meaning behind the lyrics step forward, Imagine manages to resonate from the very beginning. It's one of those songs where you don't just hear it, you feel it.I have to say also that Snoop's new mission of peace makes for much more compelling material than some of his other work. His more soulful songs bring me back to "Lil' Ghetto Boy" from the Chronic. A lot of hip-hop artists have tried to inject positivity into their rhymes and failed, mostly because they couldn't make hope and optimism as addictive as their gangster tales. Snoop on the other makes you feel like you can still have a cool swagger and still get warm booty without all the mean-mugging and gangster thuggin'. Even his more relaxed visage on the cover works much better than the wrenched up face I've seen on his other album covers. His image and his lyrics seem to project a more natural Snoop -- a perfect image since being laid back comes natural to him.As far as the five iffy tracks on this album -- whatever. You still have 16 really solid tracks remaining. I hope this isn't our last Snoop album. If anything I think this is proof that Snoop and Doc in the studio one more time will give us another good hit of the Chronic before the Detox.

reviewText: Are You Experienced?(1967). The Jimi Hendrix Experience's First Album.Before Jimi Hendrix came out with 'Are You Experienced?', he was a humble blues guitarist, who toured with bands like B.B. King, Sam Cooke, Soloman Burke, and Chuck Jackson. Fortuneatly, Hendrix thought it was in his best interest to go solo, so he moved to England, where he hired Drummer Mitch Mitchell and Bassist Noel Redding to collaborate on his first album, 'Are You Experienced?'. Hendrix took the role of lead guitarist and vocalist, exploring new sonic territories in the electric guitar, taking the traditional blues sound and speeding it up and playing it heavier, in a sense, creating Hard Rock and Heavy Metal as we know it. To this day, almost every Guitar publication names Jimi Hendrix as the greatest man to every strum a guitar. When his debut was released in England, and later in America, on both sides of the pond, the album soared to the top of the charts and spawned huge hits like 'Purple Haze', 'Fire', 'Hey Joe', 'The Wind Cries Mary', and 'Foxey Lady'. As time went on, Jimi Hendrix's debut proved to be a heavy influence on the guitar of the time, and bands like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Deep Purple expanded on what Jimi Hendrix had started, and only Eddie Van Halen can claim any influence nearly as heavy as Hendrix's. Becoming one of the most praised and well-known albums ever, I could only expect this album to be great. Was I right or wrong? Read on to find out!Track Ratings-"Purple Haze" is Hendrix's ode to marijuana, and his electric guitar sweeps out of your speakers behind his funny and mischevious lyrics. He immediately shows his talent on the guitar, with his incredible ability to create addictive riffs and multi-faceted solos. "Manic Depression" finds Hendrix doing Psychadelic Rock at his best, as he and Mitch Mitchell battle out for center-stage while Hendrix voices his "emotional problems". "Hey Joe" finds Hendrix dealing with darker subjects, telling of murdering his wife after he found her cheating. Hendrix uses a backup choir and a guilt-driven guitar lick that gives the song a more adult feeling. "Love Or Confusion" sounds similar to The Rolling Stones, and if Hendrix's vocals were actually hereable this would be an excellent song, chockful of arpeggios and solos you can barely believe existed in the 1960's. "May This Be Love" is a weird, trippy song that talks about waterfalls and finds Hendrix dishing out some clever blues licks. "I Don't Live Today" sounds like Led Zeppelin, and Jimi Hendrix and Mitch Mitchell jam out with their respective instruments in this fun rocker. "The Wind Cries Mary" is a slow blues-driven song, showing Hendrix using a pulsing electric guitar lick, which seems rather sarcastic next to his vocals. "Fire" erupts out of your speakers, with Hendrix's guitar seeming more like Aerosmith or AC/DC's, and Hendrix turns the song into a crazy party song. "Third Stone From The Sun" is an off-beat instrumental, and Hendrix takes his blues and jazz guitar to new heights, while Mitch Mitchell and Noel Redding easily stand their ground. "Foxey Lady", Jimi Hendrix's signature song, is a collection of metallic guitar licks, frequent time signature changes, and a just plain funky rhythm; gotta love it! "Are You Experienced?" is a funky, care-free song, kind of a hybrid of Iron Butterfly and The Rolling Stones; more than anything, it shows Hendrix destroying all competition on his competition. "Stone Free" is a crazy, Reggae and Psychadelic influenced song, combining an insane rhythm with Mitchell's wacky percussion, almost like Nazareth's "Hair of the Dog". Hendrix shines here yet again, and shows he was obviously a blues guitarist in his past. "51st Anniversary" is a humorous, sarcastic ode to marriage, that manages to find influences of The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Muddy Waters. "Highway Chile" is a blues rocker, featuring a gloomy guitar lick and commanding vocals from Hendrix, closely resembling Cream's "Badge" and "White Room". "Can You See Me" is a trippy blues track, finding Hendrix reaching back to his roots, and playing a funny, addictive song worthy of anything by B.B. King. "Remember" is a Psychadelic and 50's Rock influenced track, taking a low key guitar lick and putting in a rhythm not unlike in a Beach Boys or CCR song. Hendrix handles his vocals and guitar quite well, even if he's trying to mimic 50's rock(which traditionally fails in those respects). "Red House", the album's closer, is an epic *pure* Blues track, finding Hendrix wailin' about his sorrows and playin' like a madman. Throughout, Jimi Hendrix plays a guitar with a sweet and sorrowful tone you won't soon forget.Overall, 'Are You Experienced?' is a fantastic debut, showing Jimi Hendrix upping the heaviness and speed of traditional Blues to create some of the finest Hard Rock out there. Although he's not the guitarist everyone claims he is, Hendrix was alone in terms of talent for his time, and without him, everyone might still be playing like Chuck Berry and Eric Clapton. From Psychadelic, to Funk, to Blues, to Pop/Rock(a la Beatles), to R&B;/Rock, and to Hard Rock, Hendrix never falters or takes a misstep, and every track is original and creative in its own way. If you like what you've heard on the radio, or think Jimi Hendrix is overrated, get 'Are You Experienced?' or any of his other albums. I doubt you'll be unimpressed!HIGHLY RECOMMENDED TO FANS ROCK, BLUES, AND JIMI HENDRIX! ONE OF THE STRONGEST AND MOST INFLUENTIAL DEBUTS OF ALL-TIME!Killer Kuts- Purple Haze, Manic Depression, Hey Joe, The Wind Cries Mary, Fire, Third Stone From The Sun, Foxey Lady, Stone Free, and Red House.Also Recommended-Electric Ladyland- Jimi HendrixHighway 51 Revisited- Bob DylanThe Doors- The DoorsThanks For Reading!

reviewText: At the time this was released (2002), my general impression of In Absentia was that it was pretty heavy, but not overwhelmingly so.  What I like the most about this album (and band for that matter) is the emotional sophistication of the music - in combination with their solid musicianship it makes for a very rich listening experience.Musically, the band is very tight and the trademark Porcupine Tree blend of haunting and sad minor chords, fine vocals, atmospheric synthesizer parts and heaviness works very well.  I especially liked the fact that they had moved on from the slightly lighter and "poppier" sound of Lightbulb Sun (2000) - In Absentia is a very dark album overall.  Although all of the tracks are very enjoyable, my favorite is the sad piece entitled Heart Attack in a Layby.With respect to instrumentation, I enjoy the synthesizer textures that Richard uses - they are mainly used to simulate strings and are used as a sustained backdrop rather than a melody line.  The mellotron (samples?) are also quite nice. Steve's guitar textures/timbres include delicate acoustic sections, clean tones on an electric, and a thunderous, "crunchy" tone on the electric.  Overall, the contrast of the light and the heavy is quite nice and was a hallmark of the best progressive rock from the 1970s.  It is also worth noting that In Absentia features new drummer Gavin Harrison for the first time on a PT studio album - I find his overall technical approach to be very similar to the previous drummer (that is a good thing by the way).This is a great album by a very interesting post-progressive band that continues to create exciting music. For those folks interested in the bands earlier, more ambient works, excellent examples include The Sky Moves Sideways (1995) and Signify (1996).

reviewText: After listening to the "Morning View" CD a thousand times, I went out and bought this album to see what all the buzz was about. I could've picked this CD first but I was too drawn into the mellow rhythm of the "Morning View" CD that I had to get that one first to soothe my hunger. Anyway, I'm still a new Incubus fan, seeing how I just started to listen to them this year whereas back a few years ago, I used to just hear one of their songs on the radio or something. "S.C.I.E.N.C.E" is arguably the best Incubus album by many people's standards and I have to agree to a certain extent that it is, although preferably my favourite is either "Make Yourself" or "Morning View" but I won't categorize until I've heard "A Crow left of the Murder." This album is as experimental as you can get, it has an awesome blend of rock, spacey-sounds, jazz, rap and electronic and THAT'S what I call diverse. Not only that but each track delivers something special and sticks with the whole "Scientific" theme with songs like "Vitamin." My favourite songs are "New Skin," "Idiot Box," "A Certain Shade of Green," "Summer Romance (Anti-Gravity Love Song)" and "Nebula" (THIS SONG IS INSANE!). Anyway, this is one of those albums that you can just zone out with, close your eyes and take a warp trip through your mind to another planet because it's all there. This album never gets boring and there are even some hidden track sessions which I find funny. This is classic Incubus, pick it up!

reviewText: Many Tori fans see this album as good but not great, but I strongly disagree. I especially like the weird and wonderful Tori and also the electronica Tori, and this album displays a combination of both, and I also stress that this is NOT  pop album. Too many people are calling this a pop album because of the singles Bliss, Glory Of The 80s, 1000 Oceans and to a lesser extent Concertina - all of the other songs are definatly not mainstream. I don't know if this was on purpose, but it gives the album a 'mixed' and abstract feel.The album begins with the best lead single sice Cornflake Girl. It is a bit dark at the beginning but turns into an excellent popular song. Juarez follows and it is one of the least mainstream songs, with Datura. It is also one of my favourites and conveys a strong theme. Concertina follows. It is a bit 'simple' in a way, compared to the other tracks but still is very good. Track 4, Glory of The 80s was the lead single in the UK, and other countries in Europe, and although, like the previous track, it is still very good, though not one of my favourites.Lust is a fanfavourite. It is one of my favourite Tori ballads - definatly top 3, and is my third favourite on this CD. I enjoy the simplicity and weidness of the next track, Suede. I loved it the first time I heard it. It sounds to me very 'tense', sort of and I especially like the lyrics. Josephine follows and it is another ballad; Whilst it is not as good as Lust, it is still excellent.Riot Poof is absolutely awesome. It is one of my top 3 favourite Tori songs (with Yes, Anastacia and The Waitress, which is performed excellently on the live disk of this CD set by the way) and it took about 3-4 listens to really grow on me, like most of the non-singles. I especially love the bizarre ending and this is my favourite song on this CD. I never thought I would like a track better than Datura, which was the first song I heard on this CD via the Tori Amos website and Datura is now the second favourite. If you like the unusual side of Tori (hense me) this song will definatly be one of your highlights. She almost hypmotises you with the Dividing Canaan..... ending. And the abstract lyrics are very random and don't make any sense to the listener, so there will be various interpretations of this song, of course.  Spring Haze is a wise choice to follow the weird Datura, as it is also not very mainstream and another highlight. It ranks around my fourth favourite and the chorus is particularly..... good.I quite miss the way Tori used to close her albums with songs such as Little Earthquakes and Yes, Anastasia, because they are the only time Tori has closed a studio album without a slow ballad. 1000 Oceans is my least favourite on this CD but this is NOT to say that it is bad, actually, it is very good.To conclude, To Venus And Back is my second favourite TA album, my first being Boys For Pele, and the third being From The Choirgirl Hotel. Under The Pink is fourth. This is, in my opinion, Tori Amos' most underrated work DEFINATLY,  and I can't see how fellow Tori fans don't like this CD as much as most others.The live disk is also very good, but I have chosen to base this review on the studio work. The highlights on this disk are Precious Things, Cooling, with my favourite being the 10-minute long: "Waitress".95%

reviewText: Let me start out by saying that, back in 1990, when I first heard this appealing voice accompanied by a great dance-beat come forth from my radio with "C'Mon And Get My Love (With D-Mob)", I was instantly  hooked. However, I was only 12, and did not quite know who this woman was  just yet, not to mention that I wouldn't have had the money at that time to  buy her CD anyway! So I waited, and waited some more. As 1990 ended and  turned into 1991, I then heard "Just Another Dream", "Touch  Me (All Night Long)", and finally that summer, the slower-paced  romance ballad "Too Many Walls". And I even remember seeing a  little bit of the video for that last track. Unfortunatly, for a long while  through the early and mid-'90's, I thought of Cathy Dennis' music less and  less, ever since I heard "Irresistable" from her second album  "Into The Skyline" on the radio once in 1992.More on that  particular subject later, I promise.Anyway, when I finally realized that  it would be a great idea indeed to find and acquire Cathy's cool music  material on CD, I looked no further than my local pawn shop and used music  store for this great album, for one thing, like I said about the other  item, more on it later. So, now, besides the aforementioned singles, my  favorite dance songs have to be "Everybody Move", the title track  "Move To This", "Got To get Your Love", and "Taste  My Love". The other two, "Tell Me" and "My Beating  Heart" I don't care for, as they are just the wrong kind of slow song  I have never liked. All in all, this is quite the impressive dance-pop  album from the early '90's for sure.In the meantime, however, Ms. Dennis  has managed to keep herself busy with other projects. Like singing  "Find The Key To Your Life" with David Morales, on the now  out-of-print "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II" soundtrack in  1991, then she contributed "S.O.S." to the "Beverly Hills,  90210-The College Years" album in 1992, and in 1993, she performed a  romance ballad duet with Lance Ellington called "Marian", off the  also now out-of-print "Robin Hood: Men In Tights" soundtrack.Now for the earlier subject I promised to talk about. It seems that  Cathy's above-average second album "Into The Skyline" is no  longer available from this, and many other music-ordering internet sites.  But I plan to find one that does feature it, and I shall proceed to give it  yet another intelligent review as I just have for this one.By the way,  I still have yet to acquire her third Japanese Import title, "Am I The  Kinda Girl?" , which is indeed available here from Amazon.com. As soon  as I receive and have listened to it a few times, you can be sure to expect  yet another quality-filled review from me of that relatively obscure album  as well. Whew, what a time I've had typing this all out! I hope that my  opinions have helped others in choosing truly great music material in the  future! I'm gone now, bye!
summary: She is missed here in the U.S., that is for sure!

reviewText: If we could name a true '90s artist,it was Mariah Carey.  This greatest hits album is long overdue, has all of her hits from Columbia!  From Vision of Love to Heartbreaker, 28 unbelievable songs! She is a master of strong pop songs as a songwriter, as a songstylist and artist.  And she can sure hit those high notes so very good. I wished that they would have made a 20 or 32-page CD booklet of rare photos of Mariah or a written summary of Mariah's successful career,as most compilations do.
