reviewText: Released at a time when pop and soul music was inondated with rap tie-ins, D'Angelo's debut, "Brown Sugar," played like a jazzy breath of fresh air.  The followup, "Voodoo," has a bit more of a modern mindset, but D'Angelo still channels classic soul stylings and overtones to make for one of the more sophisticated R&B albums around.Early on in the album, a couple of tracks make a concerted effort to keep up with the times: the opening cut "Playa Playa" has all the cockiness and lingo of a mack daddy, while the sexual come-on "Left and Right" features explicit raps from Method Man and Redman.  This is all well and good, and the tracks are impressive and infectious...but the equally modern-sounding "Devil's Pie" is more impressive, an account of greed and excess that is at once funky and chilling, sounding like something that might have been left off Prince's "Sign o' the Times."  (Speaking of Prince, "Untitled - How Does it Feel" all but channels his Royal Funkiness in sultry ballad form.)  There's still plenty of retro stylings to be had, however, on the romantic "Send it On" and the longing "One Mo'Gin," both scorchingly soulful ballads sounding straight out of Marvin Gaye's vaults.  And of course a well-chosen 70's cover never hurt anyone...including Roberta Flack's "Feel Like Makin Love," here given an old-school horn arrangement while still managing to update its rhythms to an irresistible level.If there's a problem to be found in "Voodoo," it's lack of variety.  The Latin-tinged "Spanish Joint" and the mesmerizing "Africa" offer some rhythmic excursions, but too many of the songs feature seemingly identical drum kits and arrangements.  D'Angelo himself seemed to partly realize this, as the end of "One Mo'Gin" and "Greatdayndamornin" feature half-baked ideas tacked on to their finishes that would have been just the variation the album needs if only they had been allowed to grow into complete songs.  Make no mistake, an acoustic approach to hip-hop is a great idea, but as a result of this "The Root" (at the very least) ends up sounding barely recognizable amidst so many other similarly-arranged songs.  A better idea would have been to leave the song out altogether and put its unique guitar solo on "Greatdayndamornin," a far superior composition.Still, it's pretty hard to fault D'Angelo too heavily when comparing "Voodoo" to most sophomore releases that try too hard and end up unfocused.  The bottom line is, no matter what minor imperfections you can site, D'Angelo still offers enough soulful vocals, inventive writing, and smooth production to rise above his peers, and this is one piece of "Voodoo" that's strong enough to scare any soul veteran not yet ready to pass on his crown.

There's still plenty of retro stylings to be had, however, on the romantic "Send it On" and the longing "One Mo'Gin," both scorchingly soulful ballads sounding straight out of Marvin Gaye's vaults. And of course a well-chosen 70's cover never hurt anyone...including Roberta Flack's "Feel Like Makin Love," here given an old-school horn arrangement while still managing to update its rhythms to an irresistible level.If there's a problem to be found in "Voodoo," it's lack of variety. The Latin-tinged "Spanish Joint" and the mesmerizing "Africa&quot too many of the songs feature seemingly identical drum kits and arrangements. D'Angelo himself seemed to partly realize this, as the end of "One Mo'Gin" and "Greatdayndamornin" feature half-baked ideas tacked on to their finishes that would have been just the variation the album needs if only they had been allowed to grow into complete songs. Make no mistake, an acoustic approach to hip-hop is a great idea (at the very least) ends up sounding barely recognizable amidst so many other similarly-arranged songs. A better idea would have been to leave the song out altogether and put its unique guitar solo on "Greatdayndamornin," a far superior composition.Still, it's pretty hard to fault D'Angelo too heavily when comparing "Voodoo" to most sophomore releases that try too hard and end up unfocused. The bottom line is, no matter what minor imperfections you can site, D'Angelo still offers enough soulful vocals, inventive writing, and smooth production to rise above his peers, and this is one piece of "Voodoo" that's strong enough to scare any soul veteran not yet ready to pass on his crown.

reviewText: BROTHER BROTHER BROTHER is an album in which the Isleys soon-to-be platinum 3+3 formula really gels.  Ernie, Marvin & Chris made appearances on previous T-Neck albums, but their talents were used to recycle way too many "It's Your Thing" riffs.  This album blends the right amount of covers (the title track, "Sweet Season") and great original material ("Work To Do", "Layaway").  The 10 1/2 minute bluesy take on Carole King's "It's Too Late" is lively due to Ronald's soaring vocals and Ernie's wailing guitar.  And the beautiful closer "Love Put Me On The Corner" is perhaps the first great original Isley ballad, and a huge improvement over the insipid ballads on the GET INTO SOMETHING album.  BROTHER BROTHER BROTHER gave the Isley Brothers the sound that was used in full effect on their breakthrough album 3+3.

reviewText: More performance art or satirical commentary than the kind of album you would listen to around other people at a party (unless you happen to be throwing a very, very weird party), this release from perpetual fly in the ointment Mike Patton and his extremely talented cast and crew of musical misanthropes is a must-have completely unique example of artistic vision and good-old-fashioned smart-assery.The lengthy song "Carry Stress In The Jaw" is as good an example as any of the tracks on this huge, outrageously weird album to illustrate the abberrant strangeness and anticommercialist streak evident here. Meandering it's way through nearly any and every style of music (showtunes, jazz, film scores, thrash metal, polka, children's nursery songs, spoken word beat poetry, carnival/horror show theme music, funk, pop, psychadelia and god knows what else to call it) and clocking in at over ten minutes in length, Patton serves as surrealist ringmaster to the circus-like proceedings, introducing auditory acrobats, clowns, lion-tamers, and a sideshow freak or two before firing himself out of a cannon. Truly odd, and completely original and compelling in some undefinable way. It's almost worth buying just to have around to play when you want to freak someone out....crazy.

reviewText: The Lady of Rage was a vital component of the Chronic and Doggystyle albums. Dre knows how to bring different rappers together to produce a perfect blend of voices. The production on this album is good by the likes of DJ Premier and Daz Dillinger, but The Lady of Rage just doesn't have the talent to pull off a solo album with so few guest appearances. Only a few rappers are capable of that. The Notorious BIG...I can't think of another. Even Snoop Doggy Dogg has always relied heavily on having a large crew of rappers to back him up, and he was the front man of those two albums, not just a supporting rapper like rage was. I'm surprised Rage has made a second album. I won't be buying it. I bought this because I was in need of another Chronic/Doggystyle fix but this isn't it. I believe that music can be judged by how often you want to listen to it. I never feel like listening to this.

reviewText: This is easily my favorite Redman album, after his debut one. It is unique, original and energetic, just like any other Redman release so far. The sound quality of the prevailing majority of tracks is above average. The guest appearances are pleasant and numerous. The single of the album "i can't get in the club" is a banger and the final track "smash sumthin'" is also plain increbible. These are of course only two of the numerous highlights on the album. The major weaknesses are the over-abundance of long (and sometimes boring) skits and the lack of a serious message in all of the songs. However, this is one of Redman's better releases and definitely desrves your attention, time and respect.

reviewText: So after Demi Lovato released her album "Unbroken" in 2011, many people were disappointed because it wasn't the huge comeback album she promised and she wrote/co-wrote little to no songs on it. However, I defended her because I wasn't really expecting her to be ready to write about all her emotions just after getting out of treatment.Fastforward to now. DEMI is released and it sounds like the kind of sound Demi's known for - strong, powerful ballads, as well as some upbeat songs.Heart Attack - I'm pretty sure everyone knows this one already. It's the other side to the story of "Give Your Heart A Break". A person doesn't want to fall in love with this other person b/c if they did they'd "have a heart attack".Made In The USA - Many people have compared this song to Miley Cyrus' "Party In The USA" but other than the USA theme, I don't see the similarity at all. It's definitely catchy, but nowhere near as catchy.Without the Love - My personal favorite on the album. Someone's sending Demi mixed signals and she wonders why they keep singing her love songs when it's clear they're not together.Neon Lights - Many Demi fans I know don't really like this song but personally I think it's one of my favorites. Compares Demi and her love interest to neon lights.Two Pieces - Kind of sounds like "A Thousand Years" by Christina Perri. Two lost children are trying to find friends and they find each other.Nightingale - Demi has said this song is about one of her best friends that she lost when she was about 13 and that he's always with her, she can feel when he's in the same room.In Case - Demi sings about keeping a bunch of stuff from one of her exes who I assume ran away from her without a reason and she knows she'll have to most likely get rid of it some day but she keeps it "just in case".Really Don't Care - The "All Night Long" of DEMI. An upbeat fun piece about not caring about an ex. Also a duet with Cher Lloyd ("Want U Back").Fire Starter - Demi warns us to watch out b/c she doesn't have any fear and is not holding back for anyone.Something That We're Not - Demi's trying to just "hook up" with someone but they keep trying to be more than friends with them.Never Been Hurt - The "Unbroken" (as in the song) of DEMI. If I had to pick a least favorite from the album, it'd probably be this one. It's not that it's terrible (I don't think any of the songs on this album are terrible) but I think it's just the fact that it's so similar to the title track from the previous album (and in my opinion that track was better).Shouldn't Come Back - And then we reach the "For The Love Of A Daughter" of the album. She may fool some people into thinking it's about a really bad relationship because of the "tired of getting so mad, baby" line but the "all the birthdays you missed, I was only a kid" and emotion in her voice lets you know it's actually about her father.Warrior - This song is about her abuse as a child ("There's a part of me I can't get back, a little girl grew up too fast") and how she's never gonna get hurt by them (as in the "you" of the song) again. She also got a tattoo that said "now I'm a warrior" based on this song.All in all, I'd say this is definitely Demi's most personal and therefore best album to date. Would definitely recommend.

reviewText: Bottom-Line: "The Best of Cameo," an album that is a great starting place for anyone who wants to dive into the funky musical pool that is Cameo.As I stated in my review of Word UP!, one cannot discuss the funk-infused `80's without mentioning Cameo, a band formed in 1974 by former Julliard student Larry Blackmon and twelve of his friends.  The group released its first album in entitled Chocolate City in 1976, and followed it up with Cardiac Arrest, Ugly Ego, We All Know Who We Are and Secret Omen contained a mixture of dance (disco) and funk pieces, but it wasn't until the 1980 release of Cameosis did I sit up and take notice of the group.By the mid 1980's the group had downsized considerable to just four members (later to become just three), and in 1986 the trio released their biggest commercial and critical success, Word UP!  In addition to the title track, the album also spawned Candy and Back And Forth; the trio of songs would go on to define the Cameo sound for the next two decades.  Although this seminal album made Cameo much better known and respected, it was to represent the high water mark of their career, and in 1993 the group released the "Best of Cameo."The 14 track "Best of Cameo" contains all of the group's most memorable and commercially successful songs, including Word Up (Word Up!), Single Life, Candy (Word up!), Shake Your Pants (Cameosis), Back & Forth (Word Up!), and I Just Want To Be (Nasty). All of the tracks on CD have been re-mastered, but all retain the allure of the original recordings.This CD compilation is not to be confused with the 1999 release of the same name, which only contained 11 tracks and oddly enough was missing the group's biggest hit single Word Up!.  Nor is it to be confused with the 2002 release entitled Anthology, which contained a whopping 30 tracks, not all of them commercial and or critical successes.It goes without saying the Word Up! is one of my favorites, along with Candy, Single Life, Back and Forth and I Just Want To Be.  All of these tracks epitomize the bands unique 1980's funk drenched style sound, while still remaining relevant today.  I don't particularly care for the group's slow jams; to me they lack the smooth soulfulness I have come to expect from R&B; groups.  Most of Cameo's slower numbers seemed forced and unauthentic; the last track on the CD, It's Over is a glaring, and unsatisfying example of the group's lack of emotive vigor.  While musically viable, I didn't feel the soul connection so vital for a slow-jam to be successful--at least with me.Word Up!, along with Single Life, Candy, and Shake Your Pants are the heart and soul of "The Best of Cameo" (honorable mention to I Just Want to Be), an album that is a great starting place for anyone who wants to dive into the funky musical pool that is Cameo.

reviewText: A couple of weeks ago I saw a video in which the famous movie director Quentin Tarantino was asked about the music that he had on his iPod. Much to my (pleasant) surprise he said this album and then he went on to talk about it enthusiastically. My surprise came from the fact that not many people know this album. Which is a crying shame because it deserves more attention and praise.And it's the only Jacksons concert album officially released (I'm talking about The Jacksons, not the Jackson 5). It was recorded in the fall of 1981 on the Jacksons' Triumph Tour. It features songs from the Jacksons' Triumph and Destiny albums, and also from Michael's first solo album as an adult, Off The Wall. Plus the inevitable Jackson 5 Medley, for old times' sake.Michael sings lead vocals on all songs and he is in absolutely top form vocally. I especially love his performances on ballads, such as I'll Be There, Ben and She's Out of My Life. I love the band on this tour as well.Michael Jackson fans for years begged for a release of a concert CD by Michael, which was finally heard when in 2012 a live CD of the 1988 leg of Michael's Bad World Tour was released (as a part of the Bad 25 boxset though - not as a CD that one can buy seperately). I love that too, but this isn't any worse (I'm tempted to say the band is actually better on this one). It complements the Bad Tour CD very well, because here a different set of songs is performed - with focus on Off The Wall era material (including the two Jacksons album mentioned), while the Bad Tour set list focuses, of course, mainly on the Bad and Thriller albums.So I wish more people would discover this gem. Another secret wish of mine regarding this material is that someone would find film reels for a Triumph Tour concert and it would get a release on DVD/Blue-Ray!

reviewText: James BrownLive At The Apollo (1962-Expanded Edition CD)Recording a live show in a theatre like The Apollo in 1962 was no small feat.  The effort put into making this recording paid off in giving the world one of the greatest live albums ever made.  The mastering done for this expanded CD makes the experience even better.The concert begins powerfully with "I'll go crazy" and maintains that power all the way through to its "Night Train" ending.  Even in 1962, James Brown was known as `the hardest working man in show business', but the release of this album made him the undeniable `King of Soul'.The four Bonus tracks on this CD consist of three singles released in that period plus another short Medley.  These repeat songs already in the original live album and are, nevertheless, nice additions to the CD.This CD is beyond classic, it is an essential recording to own.  This deserves a SIXTH Star.

reviewText: If you're a Classic Rock fan, you should own this album. Really. It's loaded with rock classics such as Ramblin' Man (actually one of the lesser songs on this collection in my mind), Statesboro Blues, Midnight Rider, Dreams and Whipping Post. Plus it contains NONE of the Allman's legendary stage indulgence. Oh, that and the music's good. Highlights include Whipping Post, Midnight Rider, Statesboro Blues, Dreams, Melissa, Revival, Southbound and Crazy Love, though virtually ever song is great.However, there is a song I could've done without, and that's the completely forgettable, overlong instrumental In Memory of Elizabeth Reed. And the fact that Trouble No More and It's Not My Cross to Bear were excluded really makes me mad. But I would still recommend this highly.

reviewText: Anna Nalick's debut cd "Wreck of the Day" shows an artist who has a promising career ahead of her.  Musically, the cd has some great catchy songs and good refrains.  Lyrically, Anna has a better grasp that most of her debut peers.Her lyrics are very poetic while at the same time almos tlike a journal entry about how she's feeling.  Of course we've seen artists do this in the past, Alanis Morrisette comes to mind.  And, for a young star, her lyrics work really well.  For instance, in the song "Bleed," "And hiding beneath my blankets and sheets I'm finally free/ I'm killing the ghost of you and I'm close to awakening me" she sings in reference to trying to forget a love she left and still dealing with the hurt feelings and the desire to go back.  Other lyrics take a darker path that you can feel the pain.  For instance, "So I'm taking these pills for to fill up my soul/ And I'm drinking them down with cheap alcohol/ And you'd be inclined to be mine for the taking/ And part of this terrible mess that I'm making/ But you...you're the catalyst."  A long passage to put here, but you can feel the pain but also how poetic it sounds.Yes, it's not the greatest cd out right now.  But, what it does do is put Anna Nalick in the forefront of her peers, in my opinion.  I would rather support and listen to her grow than most of the other young female artists out there right now.  She has a good voice, a good grasp on lyrics and the arrangements keep your interest.  Overall a decent start.  Hopefully we'll hear more from her.

reviewText: Like most who sampled this, I was hooked by the askew pop tribute to X-files star David Duchovny. The ephemeral nature of pop icons probably tends to make people overlook this album as an artifact of the past decade, but that's writing Sharp off too easily. Lyrics claiming the TV spookchaser is the "American Heathcliff" and the stalkerish menace of the fadeout "I'll be waiting in Nevada" hint at the abilities Bree possesses. A listen to the album reveals an awful lot for your about $5 used.HIGHLIGHTS:"America" simultaneously castigates ("sit back, relax, enjoy the war from your living room") and celebrates ("All I know is my lonely soul and the remote control") consumerism and apathy, while "Fallen" addresses the issues of poverty and suffering viewed through the lens of a little girl's eyes, perhaps Bree's own? ("Why doesn't everyone have what they need? Where are the angels?"). While "Fallen" may be the album's strongest song, loose male harmony vocals keep the chorus from being what it could be. "Cheap and Evil Girl" puts Bree in the shoes of a femme fatale who toys with boys AND the law ("The dumb gumshoe making his rounds, shaking all the wrong girls down").LOWS:Probably the only completely lackluster tracks on this one for me are "Show Me" which seems out of place as it careens between angsty rock and formulaic pop..and "Fool's Gold" which is a by the numbers disillusionment tale.BOTTOM LINE:Better than the bargain bins you find her in...think of her as Sheryl Crow with more snarl and better lyrics in general. I'll be looking for a copy of Sharp's followup "More B.S." now...3 1/2 stars

reviewText: Unfortunately, Laura Nyro lost the battle with cancer a few years ago and left us way too soon.  Her compositions were one of the hallmarks of the 60's and on. Quite a few of the top artists covered her.  The list of acts she influenced is wide and impressive, including Rickie Lee Jones and Steely Dan."Nested" was originally recorded in 1976 when Nyro was carrying her only child.  I know "Eli and the 13th Confession" earned most of this artist's accolades, but this is my favorite of her music.I first bought "Nested" on vinyl and upgraded to a tape.  I recorded the tape to a CD and have almost given up hope of this lovely recording making it to CD. I'm grateful to see this has happened--and yes, it's worth the wait.Favorites:NestedMr. Blue (Note:  product description saying "Mr. Hue" is incorrect)Child of the UniverseRebecca Kyle, September 2008

reviewText: Still riding high on the success of 1983's "Just Be Good To Be," Atlanta's Sounds of Success create a hot follow up thanks again to the creative sounds of Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis.  The 7 track album starts off with the sensational "No One's Gonna Love You" followed by the pleading "Weekend Girl," and then the upbeat, yet romantic drenched, title track (which is the unofficial sequel to "Just Be Good To Me").  The first two songs were popular among R&B radios across the US, were later sampled a few times in 90s and early 2000s Hip-Hop music, and they peaked in the top 20 and 40 on the R&B charts, respectively.  The title track peaked at #6 on the R&B charts in the fall of 1984 and it followed with a fairy tale-esque music video that spun in heavy rotation on BET and WABC's New York Hot Tracks.  The last selection on Jam and Lewis' 4 track playlist is the funky "Break Up" which sounds like a 620 Soul Train (UK Soul Train) dance segment favorite that could rival Cherrelle's "Like I Do" which was another club dance his also produced by the Flyte Tyme duo.  The rest of the tracks (produced by the band) were ok and its fair to say that I prefer this album over the previous album, On The Rise.  Just the Way You Like It is one of 1984's misses being that it did'nt chart as well as it should.  I am glad that amazon and itunes remastered this classic because its timeless smooth production that remains consistent with the SOS Band's true sound that was still ahead of its time.

reviewText: If not for Black Rob and this album, I would consider Bad Boy a completely dead label right now, comparable to Death Row (which is also being held above water by one man--Daz Dillenger). After Cream Puffy's ever-so-wack  "Forever" late last year, and a series of release dates being  pushed back for this album, I had begun to give up hope. Singles like  "I Dare You" and "You Don't Know Me" were beginning to  get very old and played out. But then Rob drops the hit track  "Whoa!" and my eagerness to get this album was rejuvenated.And when the date finally came, after months of waiting, I was not  disappointed. The title track is a nice, but yet rugged joint showcasing  Rob's superior lyrical abilities. "Down The Line Joint" must've  been recorded quite a while ago, as it features everybody's favorite former  Bad Boy Mase. But it's still a nice track. Same with "Can I Live"  featuring former Bad Boys the Lox. The lyrics are very out-of-date, as Kiss  spits "we can't lose, cuz Puff set us up properly." But still a  good track."Thug Story" is a remake of Slick Rick's classic  "Children's Story." Rob definitely does this one justice, unlike  most remakes. And Cee-Lo stops by for a worthwhile performance on  "Lookin At Us."Rob is a great lyricist, which he shows over  and over again on this album. And the production is actually very good. The  only minor flaw I find in this is the old tracks, but even those are hard  to look down on. If this album doesn't go platinum, when artists like Hot  Boy$, Master P, and even Puff are going platinum multiple times over,  there's something wrong with the hip-hop world.Buy this album! You  won't be disappointed!
summary: Bad Boy's best release since "Ready To Die"

reviewText: It's like their hearts aren't in it anymore.  That's the only way I can put it.  Since their first three disks, it seems like the attentions of every member of this group have been everywhere but on their music, and it  shows in the quality.  All of the creativity and originality of their first  three albums (all of which are classic) is gone in this one, replaced  instead with a sort of mechanical mixing process and a gimicky second disk  which cannot be said to be anything more than a bastardized attempt at  appealing to the new in crowd.  The copious string arrangements (an idea  borrowed from such groups as Wu Tang Clan) and the hard rock edge of this  album perhaps suggest its greatest point--its irony.  It would appear that  even Cypress Hill isn't above "taking a bite" every now and then  if that's the only way to get bread...

reviewText: I pointed out in one of my guides last year that I was wondering where Norah Jones went, because she was quiet pretty much all the way through 2003. Well, my question was answered as soon as I saw the video for "Sunrise" in late January on VH1. I had been waiting for Norah to come back, and she did that and then some with her sophomore album Feels Like Home.If there are any songs that are better than the rest, they would have to be -- well, actually, it's hard to say any one song on here is better than another, but I'm gonna have to go with "What Am I to You", "Those Sweet Words", and the spiritual "Humble Me". And as usual, there are a few remakes on here, like Townes Van Zandt's "Be Here to Love Me", as well as "The Long Way Home"; the latter was originally done a few years ago by Tom Waits on the Big Bad Love soundtrack (although I never heard of that movie or any of the other artists featured on that soundtrack, either, but maybe that's just me).Another interesting thing about this album is that Norah is now expanding her vocal abilities. She doesn't try to hit any really high notes or anything, but you'll understand what I mean when you listen to songs like "Toes" and the aforementioned "What Am I to You".I gave this album four stars for one reason and one reason only: it is very hard to measure up to Come Away With Me. But that aspect doesn't take away any of the greatness of this album. Feels Like Home is right at home in my collection.Anthony Rupert

reviewText: This live album from 1980 is a rare insight on the band's marathon-tour in support of the "Tusk" album. Not only does it allow the casual listener to discover hidden gems like "Don't Let Me Down Again", "One More Night" "Fireflies" or "Over & Over", it also enables the true Mac fans to capture a milestone in the band's history.The recording is impressive; songs like "Landslide" or "Never going back again" feature such intimate readings, that you can even wonder if they were truly recorded live - that is, until a deluge of applause happens as the songs conclude. Other songs like "I'm so afraid" or "Not that funny" are a testimony to the mad genius displayed by Lindsey Buckingham on stage. Christine McVie is as good as always, with flawless performances of "Over my head" and "Say you love me". And Stevie Nicks delivers an achingly beautiful version of "Sara", less polished but more emotional than on the album version, where her voice is both sensitive and soaring. The band no longer performs "Sara" in their concerts, based on Stevie's wish, and judging from this version, one can only wonder why. This is the only official live version of "Sara" ever released, which is reason enough to purchase the album.There are plenty of high points on this album, such as "Rhiannon" (less subdued and more rocking than the version later found on "The Dance"), "Don't Stop", "Dreams", "Oh Well" and the ethereal cover of Brian Wilson's "The Farmer's Daughter". There isn't a weak moment on this album; and although it would have been nice to have songs like "Gold Dust Woman", "You Make Loving Fun" and "Songbird", it's still one of the finest live albums ever recorded.

reviewText: As I tell any friend who will listen to me, this album is hands down (along with the Allman's Fillmore and Who's Live at Leeds) one of the greatest live albums ever recorded.  The energy of this band is astounding for the year it came out--remember, the airwaves were dominated by the Beatles and Stones and Dylan.  No one could have possibly been prepared for the one-two punch of the crunching Rambling "Rose/Kick Out The Jams" (complete with notorious motherf**ker intro).  And you aren't let off the sonic ride so easily either; next is the decadent, but no less frenzied "Come Together"---in the darkness!  "Rocket Reducer No. 62" and "Borderline" continue the pace--the solo for Rocket is particularly . . . well, sonic.  "Motor City Burning" is the band's most political song, but don't listen to it for its timepiece value--listen to it for that devastating twin guitar attack of Fred Sonic Smith and Wayne Kramer; those dual solos at the same time send a shiver down my spine every time!  "I Want You Right Now" is a slow, incendiary LOUD song--it should have been the closer for this album.  "Starship" is the real closer and what a closer it is!  You can only imagine what the light show (if there ever was any) must've been like while they were blasting through this.  Their choice of a Sun Ra cover is remarkable, because it reveals a musical diversity you don't exactly glean from a first listening of this album.  Sun Ra was another true pioneer of his field; he was a jazz musician who would soberly look you in the eye and claim he was from Saturn.  His music is also 'out there'; it's no wonder that the MC5 saw in him a kindred spirit.  The only two problems a first-time listener will have will be with Rob Tyner's vocals, which are more like howls; he doesn't have an attractive voice and it takes some getting used to.  Also, "Starship" takes some patience to get through on the first and second listenings--a true freakout in every sense of the word.  If you want to know what the MC5 became after they broke up, listen to any punk band of the 70's and early 80's.  Listen to Iggy and the Stooges if you want a contemporary with the same flavor.  Listen to Patti Smith's first three albums.  Above all however, listen to the source, these guys---and play it loud!

reviewText: Bach and producer/guitarist Roy Z have teamed together to make a heavy rocking cd. this does not sound like 80's skid row. Roy Z has brought Bach up to date.The songs themselves range from pure thrash ('Angel Down') to ones with a more punky attitude and catchy chorus ('You Don't Understand') to modern 80s metal ('Love is a Bitchslap') and of course, the ballads ('Falling into You' and 'By Your Side'). Highlights also include the Zeppelin-esque 'Negative Light' where Bach pays homage to the Gods of Rock with an 'Immigrant Song' style scream. The songs with Axl Rose are great, on only one does Bach truly duet with him (the cover of Aerosmith's 'Back in the Saddle') whilst on the other two, he is in the background, perfectly complementing Bach's own voice whilst never over-shadowing him. This is mixing done to perfection.

reviewText: Twista is one of the most charismatic rappers in the game, so why doesn't this formula make a 5 star album?  Simple.  After a while this gets very boring.  Twista, while as stated earlier is charismatic, he offers no versatility.  While he can make things interesting at the beginning of the album with good songs like "Check That H**" and "Get It How You Live", towards the end you feel like you've heard to same 2 songs 14 times.  Twista tries to mix it up, going from speed rapping to speed BALLAD rapping, but like I'll admit it's very hard to pull off rap ballads.  While this works for the lead single "Girl Tonite" and even more so the with the brilliant "So Lonely" feat. Mariah Carey, it fails else where.  All in all, this is a very bland album from a terrific rapper.  At times he can be brilliant, but in the majority of the cases it's dull and often boring.  Over all, Kamikaze nor The Day After have impressed me, further enforcing my belief that Twista is more fun when he makes guest appearances on other artists songs.

reviewText: I was lucky enough to first see James Taylor live in a small outdoor venue called Avaloch in rural Lenox, Massachusetts in the summer of 1970, after this first album recorded by the Beatles in London had been released and just before the release of the fabulously successful "Sweet Baby James" album by Warner Brothers. He appeared alone on-stage with a full head of long, long hair in a simple denim shirt and cut-up jeans with his four or five acoustic guitars, and for two and a half hours proceeded to absolutely enchant the sprawling lawn-full of hundreds of audience members with a spellbinding performance of all of the work from both of those albums. Although virtually unknown at the time, word of mouth had spread so quickly in the Berkshires area (who still considers him one of their own) that many of us went out to get this album to play before he appeared. The rest, as they say, is history. Everyone there became lifelong James Taylor fans.This particular album is proof positive of Taylor's enduring ability to produce a continuing stream of memorable songs and albums. With breathless ease he delivers with such memorable new songs as "Mexico", "I'm A Fool To Care", and "How Sweet It is".  It is even more amazing considering it comes after he had already topped the charts with such extraordinary albums as "Sweet Baby James" and "Mudslide Slim", and it provides convincing evidence that our Sweet Baby James was here to stay. It, like its predecessors, is a very memorable album, and most of us who owned the original vinyl version of this album have upgraded to the CD as it has become available. It seems to showcase different aspects of his talents in that he is much more somber, reflective, and open about his own uncertainties and personal troubles in the songs he sings, and in the delivery as well. It has weathered the ravages of age very well, and it is as welcome on my CD as anything else I can think of. No one sings quite like Taylor, and it is a wonderful album to have playing as you are working your way through a quiet Saturday at home, reading or doing chores or kicking back with a Sam Adams and a few friends. Come on back to a better time, friend; sit on down with us and listen a while. This is vintage James Taylor.  How sweet it is!

reviewText: from Bruce at this stage of his career. If you're hoping to hear the Springsteen of old with the passion and creativity so prevalent on his first 6 albums you will be very disappointed. The most compelling songs are "Lonesome Day"(nice violin touch with a powerful chord structure), "Into The Fire"(you can feel it in your heart), "Empty Sky"(Bruce conveys the isolation perfectly), "Worlds Apart"(the most creative and powerful song on the cd), "Let's Be Friends"(borderline corn but Bruce pulls it off), "Your Missing"(very moving), and "The Rising"(traditional Springsteen). The worst song is "Countin' On A Miracle"(forgettable) and "My City Of Ruins" is much better than the deplorable version from the "Tribute" cd. I gave this cd 4 and a half stars not because it was a really great cd but because it was an honest effort from Springsteen to produce quality, meaningful music rather than hacking something out and selling it on his name and I appreciate that. So if you're a Springsteen fan you should buy this cd with the appropriate expectations. If you're not a Springsteen fan already this cd probably won't turn you into one. ...

reviewText: Those of you who live near the beach know that music somehow sounds different there.  The music is inextricable from the sound of softly lapping blue-green water, the smell of soft drinks and sandwiches; the warm  sand between your toes, the clink-clanking of ice cubes, the wafting of  music from a thousand small speakers mixing into the fresh light-wind, and  the promise of mystery women and men strolling, running, frisbeeing,  seemingly floating along the dry/wet sand.It's the feeling you'll get  from kd lang's new CD, no matter what the season, or your proximity to a  beach. kd's familiar brilliance envelops each song, her delivery is warm,  strong, aching, and personal. Her voice is sometimes just a bit lighter  here, and that fits the theme.  But this is not lightweight fare: Her rich,  nuanced voice conveys love-soaked emotion like no other.I enjoyed every  song, some more than others, but each jeweled by kd's honey-warm voice. The  highlights are "extraordinary," a sweet uptempo song with highly effective  overdubbing of kd, and an arrangement that nods discretely to the great  pre-Beatles groups of the 60's (and a bit of the Lovin' Spoonful).  It's  just one of many many delights here. "Love's Great Ocean" reveals the CD as  a paean to water--not summer--flowing, crashing water; seductive and  merging boundaries:  "Love's great ocean came crashing down on me,  overflowing with possibility..."The opening "Consequences" captures the  rhythms of undulating seaweed, and "It's Happening With You" has a slightly  psychedelic, Donavan feeling until it hits the bright bridge.  The song  moves and celebrates movement: Splashing, launching a frisbee, running with  your dog, it leaves a stream of images like the best of summer days. "Every  turn I take, becomes a piece of cake.  No matter what I do, it's happening  with you.""Summerfling" has a great early 60's sound (complete with  "ba-ba ba-ba-bahs," a bit of surf guitar, and organ-like sounds  complementing and pushing the beat): "Early morning, mid- July,  anticipation is making me high."  It's a faster song that recalls the Beach  Boys and the great grrl groups, but it remains wholly kd. There are hints  of surf guitar and organ-like sounds here (and elsewhere on the CD), I wish  there were more! This and "When We Collide" (the later with a convincing,  happily vanquished, take-me-now hook and joyous guitar-work) should get  plenty of airplay. filteredReviewText: Those of you who live near the beach know that music somehow sounds different there. The music is inextricable from the sound of softly lapping blue-green water, the smell of soft drinks and sandwiches; the warm sand between your toes, the clink-clanking of ice cubes, the wafting of music from a thousand small speakers mixing into the fresh light-wind, and the promise of mystery women and men strolling, running, frisbeeing, seemingly floating along the dry/wet sand.It's the feeling you'll get from kd lang's new CD, no matter what the season, or your proximity to a beach. kd's familiar brilliance envelops each song, her delivery is warm, strong, aching, and personal. Her voice is sometimes just a bit lighter here, and that fits the theme. But this is not lightweight fare: Her rich, nuanced voice conveys love-soaked emotion like no other.I enjoyed every song, some more than others, but each jeweled by kd's honey-warm voice. The highlights are "extraordinary," a sweet uptempo song with highly effective overdubbing of kd, and an arrangement that nods discretely to the great pre-Beatles groups of the 60's (and a bit of the Lovin' Spoonful). "Love's Great Ocean" reveals the CD as a paean to water--not summer--flowing, crashing water; seductive and merging boundaries: "Love's great ocean came crashing down on me, overflowing with possibility..."The opening "Consequences" captures the rhythms of undulating seaweed, and "It's Happening With You" has a slightly psychedelic, Donavan feeling until it hits the bright bridge. The song moves and celebrates movement: Splashing, launching a frisbee, running with your dog, it leaves a stream of images like the best of summer days. "Every turn I take, becomes a piece of cake. No matter what I do, it's happening with you.""Summerfling" has a great early 60's sound (complete with "ba-ba ba-ba-bahs," a bit of surf guitar, and organ-like sounds complementing and pushing the beat): "Early morning, mid- July, anticipation is making me high." reviewText: Brian Wilson envisioned this album as his masterpiece, and he's right. This album showed a side of the Beach Boys we had not yet experienced. Songs from the heart, the tight harmonies, and a beauty that few knew they were capable ofall graced the mono grooves of the original LP. Brian initially intended this album to be released only in mono, so he could have more control over what the listener heard. There was a "Duophonic" fake stereo version, but it sounded just that way. When the original multitrack master tapes were found, the process to create the stereo version was painstaking, but was well worth the effort. Now, those same master tapes allowed for the creation of a new, 4.1 surround version. I say 4.1 because the center channel is not used for the most part. But in the same way the stereo version added new textures to the sound, so does the surround mix. While it may have its critics, the combination of the surround sound and high resolution 24 bit, 96 kHz digital sound makes for a new experience with this fine album. Hats off to the folks at Capitol, and to the engineers who did such a bang-up job of making a great album even better. For those who don't yet have a DVD-Audio player, the DTS track is highly recommended.

reviewText: I never got into Jay-Z until "Hard Knock Life."  I just recently bought "Reasonable Doubt."  Jigga can put out quailty albums...when Jigga wants to.  Let's go down the list: Reasonable Doubt (8/10), Vol. 1 (7/10), Vol. 2 (5/10), Vol. 3 (6/10), Dynasty: Roc-la-Familia (8/10), Blueprint (9/10) and his latest release, Blueprint 2 (5.5/10).  So, it appears that when Jay-Z talked about Nas's album quality over the year's, he was also indirectly talking about his own albums, at least to me.Lyrically, Jay comes correct nine times outta ten.  For every five "Takeover's," there's at least one "'03 Bonnie & Clyde."  On "Blueprint," Jay doesn't drop the ball with lyrics.  He's on point from beginning to end.  "Takeover" is a tight battle track with Jay-Z spittin venom at Prodigy and Nas.  Everyone's heard this song, so there's no need to go into specifics.  The tightest track, lyrically, has to be "Renegade," but not because of Hova's two verses.  Eminem dropped two hot to death verses that were two of the best in 2001.Only two things keep this album from getting "five-mic" status: "Jigga That Ni**a" and "All I Need."  Production wise, these are the weak spots on the album.  Whack-masters...i mean...Track-masters produced the former, which is no more than a good club beat.  I guess i'm still bitter at Tone & Poke since the "It Was Written" debacle.  "All I Need" is an okay track, but it's neither a bump-able track or a laid-back, chillin out track.  Should've been tweaked once more before it was put on the album.In the end, people made too much of a fuss over this album being a classic.  Jay-Z has never released a "classic" album that is comparable to the likes of "Aquemini," "Illmatic," or "Enter the 36 Chambers."  To be honest, Jay is nothing more than a successful, commercialized pop rapper.  But that doesn't mean I won't blast "The Ruler's Back" down my block each day.

reviewText: Since her 8-Grammy win in 2003, Norah Jones has gone on to become the world's most unlikely superstar. Her debut album "Come Away With Me" was 2003's biggest selling album around the world, shifting and unprecedented 17 million copies worldwide - quite a difference from the 10,000 Norah said she would be satisfied to sell. All this without hype or airplay - rather impressive. Her blend of laid-back melodies and soothing vocals have made her a household name and her adorable face and warmly attitude have contributed to this. She's also a woman who you feel would do no wrong. She seems like a friend to her fans - a true and humble goody girl, and we all know the public loves those.Come Away With Me was released in early spring 2002 on Blue Note, a jazz label. Two years later it is still riding high in the Billboard charts, pressing down on its 110th week on the chart and close to selling 9 million copies Stateside. So it came with no surprise that the whole world's anticipation for the follow-up was nothing short of stratospheric. The album finally arrived in February 2004, "Feels Like Home" was the title, and gargantuan sales were ensured. Sure enough the album stormed to No.1 in 16 countries around the world, including the US where it shifted a staggering 1,022,000 copies in seven days - only the second album by a female artist to do so after Britney in 2000. The big question remains: does Feels Like Home live up to its predecessor?The simple answer is no it does not. Come Away With Me was a landmark album, the biggest selling jazz album of all time and no doubt a classic. Every song was a beautiful composition with seductive lyrics and sweet vocals. The same can be said for Feels Like Home, but on a less grander scale. Norah certainly hasn't messed with the formula here which is very wise, but the song's don't hit you as hard as those on her debut, yet it's still a fantastic album that will grow on you. Take the first single, "Sunrise," which opens the album. A soft and soothing beat plays melodically as Norah introduces her sunlight vocals and harmonizes the chorus to irresistible addiction. "What Am I To You?" continues this trend but adds a country twang to the verses. "Those Sweet Words" has to be one of the most beautiful songs I have ever heard. You could just imagine Norah out in a desert or a field with her lover and no one to bother them, as she questions him on what he said - did he say those sweet words or not?"Carnival Town" is one of the most relaxing and chilled songs on the album as Norah sings of attractions in a town. It sounds strange but it's beautiful and as she sings, "Is it lonely?" you realise just how in love with this woman you really are. "In The Morning" is a much more upbeat affair in which the beat gathers pace and Norah's vocals rise and fall to the composition. Another great song. "Be Here To Love Me" has a stomping beat that works very well with Norah's vocals. She sings in a very bluesy moody about love in a country way as her vocals are drawn out more and more to make another standout. "Creepin' In" is one of the most uptempo songs on the album and features, unfortunately, Dolly Parton. Yeah, we all know Dolly's a country legend, but I really can't stand her Barbie-like vocals! No disrespect to her, but this is the worst song on the album for me. "Toes" drags the album back up on top form as Norah sings of her toes just touching the water as the piano and drums play melodically in the background. Another brilliant track."Humble Me" is the longest song on the album, in which Norah sings of giving birth to a child. The father has deserted her, and she's now all alone - she turns to God for support and he responds. This is perhaps the most beautiful song on offer here, and the way it is so relaxed and emotional makes it so. A highlight for sure. "Above Ground" is another good song, with a very jazzy chorus - very sexy. Norah's vocals are incredibly seductive at this point. "The Long Way Home" has a plodding beat to begin with and is almost acoustic when Norah is singing - if it weren't for that guitar it certainly would be! "The Prettiest Thing" is just another fabulous and melodically beautiful song in which Norah addresses the prettiest thing she ever did see. The songs seems a bit awash in the rest of these brilliant songs, but it stands out after a while. The album then closes with "Don't Miss You At All" which is very similar to "The Nearness Of You" which closes Come Away With Me. A beautiful song to close the album - I could imagine listening to it as the snow gently falls outside my window in the winter.OVERALL GRADE: 10/10Norah has recently said in a magazine article, "Look, I get why people like my music. It's easy to listen to. It's easy to digest. It's not offensive. I get it. It's also not genius." She's spot on here. When you think about the compositions of Norah's songs, they're not exactly breaking any ground, but what they are doing is giving the public something to adore, something to treasure and something to believe in. Is there anything wrong with that? Hell no. Norah Jones is living proof that you can make simple music with basic instruments and catchy melodies. Doing it well like she does appeals to the masses and provokes a reaction in millions of listeners all over the world. Feels Like Home confirms this, as well as proving Norah's staying-power in the music industry.

reviewText: The average listener really doesnt know Aerosmiths debut album. Hell, few average listeners know classic early 70's Aerosmith to began with. But even the most commercial music fan who likes Jamies Got a Gun, Love In An Elevator, Dude, or Rag Doll is aware of some of the hits off the bands early records, this album however is devoid of airplay aside from one major song and maybe a little bit of another. Those bring Dream On and Mama Kin. But is their debut any good? Most call it uneven but AS fans even hard rock fans at least find a few gems on this debut album.The truth is, it is a great album. There arent many stand out cuts on it. It's more of an album you play the whole way through. Make It, Somebody, One Way Street and Write Me are all competant rock songs, infused with that youthful energy and Stones-ish swagger. These guys definatly know what they're doing. Aerosmith were one of the most important bands of the 70's. Along with Zeppelin, Sabbath, the Who and Alice Cooper they started the idea of "album rock", songs that generally werent big singles but were so good, they warranted airplay for longer tracks, this of course mainly being served up on what was at the time the underground FM radio. This first album finds the boys out of Boston, trying to find their sound, sure it's underdeveloped but theres hints of what would become in not too long. Movin' Out has a famaliar riff and is a good song as well, but its the final song, a cover of Rufas Thomas' Walkin The Dog that really cooks. Previously done by the Stones (no surprise there), Aerosmith really brings the whole album together with this rocklicking barn burner.As with most debut albums, there's always the band trying to find what theyre looking for, laying down those tracks they had been playing in smokey bars and clubs for the last year. Mama Kin is of course the energetic rocker that a few years later would finally become a recognizable track but it was Dream On that was the albums major sell point. Of course when released in early 72, it wasnt a hit. Most people dont realize it wasnt until around late 75/early 76 the song was re-released after the band were superstars and become one of thier staple tracks, it was actually on their debut. While Aerosmith is often cited as a major influence on the birth of American heavy metal, that MIGHT be so, but the band was way more steeped in the blues and Stones' style party till you die swaggering to be considered in along with Ozzy and the boys. This album may not appeal to everyone but for those curious as to where Aerosmith got their start, and a great slice of early 70's American rock n roll, check this record out.

reviewText: "Little Queen" (1977) #9  extra tracks (2004).2nd album by the Wilson Sisters.  This is a departure from their debut album, there are more acoustic laced numbers like, "Love Alive", "Treat Me Well" and "Cry To Me".  You also get the mandolin music of "Sylvan Song" and "Dream Of Archer", brings to mind early 70's Led Zeppelin.  And then you get the hits, hard rockers, "Barracuda" #11 hot 100, "Kick It Out", #79 hot 100 and the mid-tempo title track #62 hot 100.  You also get the whimsical "Say Hello".  On the extra tracks we get "Too Long A Time", another version of "Love Alive" and a good rendition of Zeppelin's "Stairway To Heaven", live.  Just as good as "Dreamboat Annie", just a little softer.  Great album cover, Ann and Nancy look really good here.  "Magazine" followed this about 6 months later.

reviewText: I personally would recommend buying Jill Scott's sophomore opus "Beautifully Human (2004)" FIRST.But you can't go wrong starting with this album if it's indeed your intro to Jill Scott.Who is Jill Scott?An around the way girl from North Philly whose as strong, feminine, positive and real as any black female singing talent since Mary J. Blige.Oh, and did I mention this girl can SANG?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?"Gettin' in the Way," was the song that introduced her to the world ... this black women's anthem to handling the "other woman."  It's sassy and jazzy at the same time.Yet, "A Long Walk" -- her second single -- was the song that won me over.You gotta remember that circa fall 2000/spring 2001 the neo soul movement was running strong in the United States with Erykah Badu dropping "Mama's Gun," D'Angelo back out with "Voodoo" plus debuts from India.Arie, Angie Stone and Musiq Soulchild.This album will make you remember that time more than anything, though I honestly believe Jill's second album "Beautifully Human" is the better album because there's EVEN MORE JILL -- more substance, more love of self and love of life.If Mary J. Blige = modern day Aretha Franklin and Erykah Badu = modern day Billie Holiday, then Jill's gotta be a modern day Ella Fitzgerald.If you like any and all of these singers, you're gonna love Jill Scott.

reviewText: In a world where there are seemingly endless Britneys and Christinas emerging on the pop scene, it is overwhelmingly refreshing to come across a fully-clothed, talented young woman who plays guitar and sings with soul. This is exactly what you will find on Michelle Branch's debut album, "The Spirit Room". Full of brilliantly-crafted tracks, the record is one that will live on beyond the studio creations of other pop princesses.Sounding more mature than her years, Branch brings to mind what a young Sheryl Crow or Meredith Brooks sounded like. Every track here is edgy, with a rocky vibe and catchy refrain. Rather than go through each and every song, I'll give you the highlights:'Sweet Misery': Taking a cue from '80s ballads like 'Time After Time', 'Sweet Misery' is a both touching and memorable look at the bitersweet feelings love can evoke.'Goodbye to You': One of Michelle's more mellow tracks, 'Goodbye to You' paints an accurate picture at what a breakup is like - not angry but painful.'All You Wanted': A radio hit, this track is a bit more pop than the other songs on the album, but still contains the rocky flavor felt throughout.'You Set Me Free': Another radio hit, this song is both infectious and irresistible. Featuring an addictive guitar riff and brilliant vocals, it is truly a great recording.With all of the over-produced garbage on the airwaves today, artists like Michelle Branch prove that true music is still out there. And if you're looking for a great musical experience, go no further than this record.

reviewText: This may be my favorite live album from back when vinyl albums ruled the day.  There are certainly a handful of live albums which capture the spirit  of THE place to be (like Aretha at the Filmore, among others).  Back in the  day, just about every night at the Apollo was the place to be.  This was  never more true than when James was in the House, without a doubt.This  album just whets the appetite for more of the Godfather of Soul.  His J.B.  Fast Medley (almost a redundancy considering his work) is a phenom.  This  has a lot of his late 60's, early 70's classics, like Super Bad, Hot Pants,  Sex Machine, Get Involved, and a handful of others that make you just want  to move.The crowd screaming, clapping and singing along (actually, more  like yelling, considering who has the lead) helps generate some of the  excitement that seeing J.B. live holds.  Be forewarned though, there is  NOTHING like seeing J.B. live.  No live album can do him the true justice.  Better appreciated, I think, by those who have some familiarity with the  studio cuts.  Still no doubt great stuff.

reviewText: I'm glad to see that a complete collection of Elton John is finally put out.  However, it does miss a few essential tracks.  It does not have "Lucy in the Sky", "Pinball Wizard", "Mama Can't Buy You Love", or "Blue Eyes", which many would argue that are important EJ tracks.Another couple of disappointing things about this collection is that "Saturday Nights Alright for Fighting" fades out nearly a minute early, and "Daniel" sort of fades as it ends which makes the start of "Saturday Night..." a little more harsh following it.  "Sorry Seems To be the Hardest Word" ends Disc One and "Don't Go Breaking My Heart" starts Disc Two.  This is kind of annoying, since these two tracks would be better reversed in the collection.  And chronologically, it should be. Remember, the first disc covers EJ's first and strongest 6 years of his era, and the second disc covers his last 26 years.  I like to shuffle my discs when I listen to them, so having "Don't Go Breaking My Heart" and "Sorry Seems to Be the Hardest Word" really sounds out of place on each disc.On the second disc, "I Don't wanna Go On With You Like That" is out of place if you consider that these tracks are supposed to be in chronological order.  However, when you consider the intensity of its upbeat sound, it would sound kind of out of place if it were placed between "Nikita" and "Sacrifice".  So, I can understand why they did this.Of course, Elton John does have alot more hits (many Top 20) that have not been put in this collection, but, this collection is pretty tight for all the great songs that are here.  I don't know how high the last three tracks charted, I hope they were big hits so that the other EJ hits that were left off is justified.  The third bonus disc is kind of unecessary.  Although they could have put some more of his lower charting tracks on it.I'm not too crazy about the packaging, since this is not a standard jewel box that is usually used.  These cardboard dig-paks get tethered and worn too quickly.But, for the most part.  This is a collection worth owning, even if you have all his seventies albums on CD.  The second disc really is a bargain for Elton John fans who have his first 6 years covered.

reviewText: PRESTO is the second record produced during Rush's pop period (1987-91) and is the most successful. Despite a couple of lulls, this is one of the strongest sets of songs that the band ever came up with. I'm not sure if they are RUSH songs, but they're good nonetheless.The album opens with a bang. "Show Don't Tell" is probably Rush's best pure pop song. Who thought they could get funky? "Chain Lightning" is almost as good and "The Pass" is one of Rush's more inspired ballads. Finally, "War Paint" is a little silly, but who can resist the coda with the "boys and girls together paint the mirror black" bit. About as shamelessly catchy as Rush has ever gotten.After that the record is a little more hit or miss. There is nothing that bothers me, but some of it is kind of forgettable. Still "Superconductor" is catchy and memorable, "Red Tide" is great despite its silly production, and "Available Light" is a fine track to end on. I kind of like the title track, but if you asked me to hum any of it except for the  "if I could wave my magic wand" bit I'd be stumped.Fans of heavy progressive rock probably won't find much here to love. The crazed instrumental breaks are minimized (if not completely missing) and most of the songs clock in at under 5 minutes. If you are interested in Rush's pop period however, this would be the place to start.
summary: The best of the Rush "pop" albums

reviewText: After having found the main objects of desire at Amoeba the Eels "Hombre Lobo" and  Arcade Fire "Funeral" both on vinyl, I was already content and ready to leave when glancing trough the aisles I came across this Gomez entry. Interestingly enough it had been the previous year at Amoeba when I had found Five Men In A Hut (DVD) which introduced me to the band for the first time. Call it destiny or just mere coincidence but it was now that I was meant to hear a full Gomez album. Next thing I know more than a hour had already passed by and I was at the hotel parking lot zombie-like listening to "Bring it On". For the next week Gomez would accompany me through California all the way down to the Mexican border where "Tijuana Lady" would resonate more clearly under the dry sun. As a music lover we tend to sometimes look for relations within genres so when asked how a band sounds we would say is like a mix between this and that but with the style of that one. Well with Gomez I'm neither able or willing to create such relations. Gomez simply sounds like Gomez so to discover its every layers you'll just have to jump on it and swim in it for a while. Uniqueness a rare disease these days.

reviewText: This record, possibly more than any other Streisand release, shows Streisand's soul. The songs have that extra bit of depth to them, showing that Babs can really dig deep and produce some powerful stuff. It's Barbra's turn at R&B done her way, and she hangs with the best of them. "Love In The Afternoon" is a sweet ballad, with the aforementioned soul ringing throughout. "Guava Jelly" is Barbra trying her hand at some tropical music, with excellent congas, percussion, and steel drums.She turns in a distinctive performance of Bill Withers' "Grandma's Hands," while the mid-tempo "Jubilation" continues the funky theme with an added choir. The highlight of the record is "Simple Man," beautifully arranged with acoustic guitar, piano, and cello. Streisand voices her longing, exclaiming "I just wanna hold you/I don't wanna hold you down/I don't wanna make it on my own." The album runs from humorous to deep, while showing a more spiritual side to the Funny Girl.

reviewText: There isn't much I can add to the other reviews. But I don't intend to. I'm not trying to top what others wrote. All I want to do is plead with you to buy this CD.On The Man Comes Around, the last album Johnny Cash recorded before he died, the 70-year-old legend unleashes some of his most personal songs, plumbing the depths of his soul and singing with such palpable emotion that every song draws you in, commands your attention. And your respect.Overall, The Man Comes Around is more melancholy, more introspective than his previous three albums on Rick Rubin's American label. The pace is slower, and the feelings more obviously on his sleeve."Hurt" is a video that I can't watch without choking up. Ditto for the song itself. And "In My Life" by the Beatles. Maybe the legendary Man in Black knew his life was drawing to a close. Or maybe he was just in a sentimental mood.Whatever the reason, I have a hard time listening to The Man Comes Around without feeling waves of emotion wash over me -- made even more intense knowing he died a year after this album was released.Thank you, Rick Ruben, for allowing Johnny Cash to shine on your record label.To everyone reading this review, if you haven't done so already, please buy The Man Comes Around.

reviewText: Every time I play it I enjoy Basement Jaxx's latest effort more and more. Taking on a whole lot of possible meanings (and influences) 'Kish Kash' (a mutation of the hebrew term for "internal organs", and the Middle Eastern slang for "money") represents the DJ duo comeback with a more mature and substance-filled approach. The album blends influences and tempos like you can't imagine, and does a better job at it than last year's very eclectic 'The Richest Man in Babylon' by Thievery Corporation.Particularly appealing about the album is the HEAVY influence of funk and soul that can be felt through most of it with the opening "Good Luck" (with Gladys Knight-like vocals and guitars a-la-Curtis Mayfield all comingling in the most organic fashion) as the epitomizing track of it all. The album also highlights 'cooler' songs like "If I Ever Recover", "Tonight" and "Living Room", for those that'd rather chill out than get up and dance.All in all, it's one of the best efforts in the dance segment so far this year, surpassing Groove Armada's "Love Box" and getting pretty close to BT's "Emotional Technology". In sum, a keeper!
summary: 4.5 stars: More mature, becomes more enjoyable w/each listen

reviewText: If you're like me, you probably didn't feel like reviewing this album for at least a month.Like most here, I'm a fan who's followed Kate since the 'Kick Inside' debut and have enjoyed the journey. Kate seems to be an artist who refuses to stand still so for us to wish for another 'Hounds of Love' or 'The Dreaming' is kind of pointless and perhaps ultimately an album that merely treads old territory would've had very little to say.Kate Bush's work is fundamentally emotional, as evidenced by her sad and lost album 'The Red Shoes' and perhaps she withdrew after that album for fear that she exposed too much of herself, occuring as it did with the time of her relationship breakdown and her mother's death. These things are not for public consumption and it might have seemed untrue to enter immediately into another album after grappling with all of that.Having said all of that Aerial is basically a minor masterpiece. If you love Kate, you will love Aerial (although perhaps not straight away!). It takes time to discover - the album has a structure which mirrors the 'Hounds of Love', one half of solidly crafted pop songs, the other a conceptual opus. Both, in my mind are successful and I am finding myself returning to both with equal pleasure. Her musical compositions are exquisite and beautifully played - the piano parts are more refined and complex than ever. The arrangements are also brilliant and rich. Many of the reviewers here who complain of Kate not hitting the right notes with her vocals are not hearing the alternate scales being played with, and the funky play with rhythm. I haven't heard a note wrong yet. In fact the more you play the record, the more right it sounds which suggests that it is actually teaching us to hear new ways into music - a great gift indeed!A lot of the new songs also have great rhythm - take for example 'King of the Mountain', 'How to be Invisible' (where Kate seems to be having fun with people who see her as a recluse), 'Joanni' and the magnificent screaming, driven 'Aerial', the one moment on the new album which really recalls the impassioned madness of 'The Dreaming'.In a way, all of the Kate's you've come to know are on this album, there is both innocence and world weariness. I won't attempt interpret the themes of Kate's songs here as she seems to purposely leave them open for the audience's subjectivity. I should mention however, that with topics such as mathematics, celebrity, Joan of Arc, motherhood, death and domesticity, the album's thematic arc is rich and fascinating.The downside of Kate has always been the flip side of her strength - it seems to relate to her honesty as an artist. Sometimes she over-exposes herself and it can often be cloying and even uninteresting to others. 'Mrs Bartolozzi' on disc one is a perfect example, a study of cleaning that makes some weep and others run for cover. The chorus is merely Kate singing 'washing machine' over and over. Personally, the simplicity of this became intense for me, and for that reason alone I found it interesting. Kate's lyrics play with intelligent themes but they are often purely emotional journeys and those looking for deep messages might find it easy to criticize. My advise to them would be to look further for the beauty in the music and the integrity of Kate's voice. It is all a fragile experience for a listener. I've noticed that Kate has played with her voice and mixed it back often to obscure the lyrics and it actually works quite, well, using her voice more as an instrument than departing great wisdom through words which always seem quite limited in her work.There are moments of pure bliss here, perhaps particularly on disc 2 'A sky of honey' where Kate paints sonic pictures of pure tranquility and sings with perfect grace 'What a lovely afternoon...'.On a purely selfish note, I would love to see Kate write an instrumental album using voices but not lyrics, I think it would be the most pure form of experiencing the pleasure of her music.
summary: Kate Bush looks back, and forward...

Rick Rubin does a phenominal job of letting Cash express himself clearly without the mask of overproduction.This is Johnny Cash stripped to the bone, waiting for you to join him on this dark ride.

reviewText: An underrated and very interesting record, "Homebrew" is a fine effort that wisely captures the musical zeitgeist of the early nineties. Creative and diverse, Neneh Cherry`s sophomore release combines pop, soul, rap, dance, spoken-word and, most importantly, is one of the first albums that presents some songs that origin the genre known as trip-hop. Although a bit uneven, this is still a landmark record that manages to be relevant today. Some of the hip-hop oriented tracks are a tad dated now, but the electronic and sophisticated ballads "Move With Me", "Peace in Mind", "Somedays" and "Red Paint" are as excellent as ever. An unnoticed gem worth discovering, "Homebrew" as much to recommend.Worthwile music.

reviewText: The first concert I ever went to happened to be a John Denver concert, where he performed in front of giant screens that showed pictures of nature and my girlfriend had to explain to me what that strange smoky smell in the air happened to be.  This 1975 "double-album" show cases Denver at his best, with live performances of basically every hit he had up to that time, from "Take Me Home, Country Roads" to "Farewell Andromeda (Welcome to My Morning)" and "Thank God I'm a Country Boy."  The concert was recorded at the California Universal Amphitheater in August-September of 1974 and is actually a typical performance because Denver is being backed by an orchestra this time around.  The boys in the band are Steve Weisberg on guitars, Dick Kniss of bass, Herb Lovell on drums, Hal Blaine doing percussions, and John Sommers filling in on everything from guitar and banjo to fiddle and mandolin.There is a sort of thematic arrangement to the songs, which clearly show the various strengths of Denver's music.  Beginning the concert with "Farewell Andromeda" seems an obvious choice ("Welcome to my morning, Welcome to my Happiness"), but notice how he uses humorous songs like "Toldeo" and "Grandma's Feather Bed" to set up the pathos of the beautiful "Annie's Song."  Ballads are used to set up the more powerful songs, such as "The Eagle and the Hawk."  The only thing this live album reaffirms for me is that John Denver's best songs were never his big hits from the pop charts but songs like "Poems, Prayers, and Promises."  Two songs, "Today" and "Boy from the Country," are omitted from the CD reissue for time reasons, but since they are a pair of minor covers it is not a painful loss.  Even with those losses "An Evening with John Denver" is a superb live album, one of the best of the Seventies and a good addition to your music library regardless of how many John Denver albums you currently have in your possession.  For me, there is the added advantage of this being pretty much the concert I remember hearing back then (probably Fall of 1973, maybe the spring of 1974).

reviewText: The Mariah Carey of 20 years ago is nothing like the Mariah Carey of the present day. Who knew the shy, slim, curly haired 20 year old from Long Island who belted out Vision of Love and danced in a field to Dreamlover would ditch her clothes and rub elbows with rappers on Honey? The journey is well worth a listen. Blessed with a velvety five octaved voice and piercing whistle register that could shatter glass and make dogs howl, it was obvious Mariah was destined to be a star. She later married her manager Tommy Mottola and the hits kept on comin'. Emotions, I'll Be There, Hero, Fantasy. After leaving her hubby, the hair got longer and the "ensembles" got shorter. Butterfly, the album and the song, was a reference to her divorce from Tommy and the freedom to take more control over her career. Some hot pants and roller skates later, Glitter! Let's not go there. Her former label Sony released a double disc of all the hits and it's the perfect choice for anyone who wants a more complete compilation of her songs pre-Glitter. The packaging is pretty skimpy (insert Mariah joke here) with no liner notes, but who needs that when you've got the tunes?

reviewText: Led by lazy-eyed frontman Colin Hay, Men at Work is to Australia's popular music as "Mad Max" is to Australian film--about as good as it gets.  They rock by way of Sting and the Police, with less-obvious reggae influences, less grit, more humility (and kook), and more showmanship (i.e. a few too many keyboards).  But they rock well, very well, even, most of the time.  Hay's lyrics are pointed, impressive, almost poignant on "I Can See It in Your Eyes."  Bandmembers Greg Ham, who plays the woodwinds and brass instruments (!), and Ron Strykert, the guitarist, contribute similarly effective songs. reviewText: I remember when I first saw the music video for GIRL U WANT - harnessing rock-n-roll songcraft to their own twisted electro/punk, they had clearly made a bold leap forward - or back? - to grab that big brass ring on Top 40 charts.  But when you listen to FOC now, along with its clutch of visionary, seminal yet bargain-basement cheap videos, you realize just how UNDERRATED DEVO ARE in the scheme of things - what other band was/is in such utter control of their creative vision, from songs, to costumes, to videos, to merchandise, to stage show, to sensibility/design/philosphy?  Looking at the landscape of empty pop drivel in 2004, it's easy to forget back in the early 80s when pop still had IDEAS to spare.  Many many great SONGS. Period. Doubt me?  Listen to a few bars of GIRL U WANT, GATES OF STEEL, COLD WAR, SNOWBALL, ITS NOT RIGHT, or the title track and just TRY to get them outta your head?!  Even better was the "Live" mini-EP rush released at the time - you can find it re-issued on Rhino Handmade in all its glory - look for it! **And don't get me started on DEVO's amazing TV appearance on ABC's long-lost answer to SNL, Fridays - who remembers DEVO's in-studio takes on GUW and GOS?  If you saw them, you know THE MEN WHO MAKE THE MUSIC.

reviewText: No one has written a satisfactory review of this vitally important album  yet, so I will make my best attempt at one.First off, this is Shellac's  best album... ever... even if they go on to make 100 more albums, this is  it, the pinnacle, the height of success.  The others are alright, this one  trumps em all.And, as Big Black were, Shellac is meant to appeal to your  sense of harsh, steady minimalism.  What you have is music that is centered  around the rhythm.  The beat is everything here, and the beat is not  complex, or wanky, or drum-solo-esque, the beat here is rock-solid.  The  bass and guitar complement the beat.  That's all, just 3 guys, the  occasional repetitious soupcan vocal, and a beat.  Now that beat does  mutate, changing when you least expect it, made all the more sneaky with  the hallmark Shellac repetition.And that's the key: repetition.  Hypnotic, hammer-pounding, steady, repetition.  It's like the simplicity of  punk rock, taken to an extreme, yet still musical.  It doesn't dazzle you  with wanky solos, or self-consciously sappy lyrics.  It strives to provide  that "bulldozer advancing down the road" heaviness, coupled with  a severely ironic, yet never pretentious, lyrical quality.It is a  dream-come-true for those who appreciate the forceful minimalism of punk  rock, yet it would not be classified as punk by any who hear it.  I  recommend taking a listen before you buy, as people whose ears are  accustomed to music with lush string arrangements and glossy production  soundscapes will likely be taken aback by the apparent simplicity of it  all.  But then, their head starts bobbing rhythmically, they start to hum a  few bars, then it hits em: there's more to this than meets the eye!

The bass and guitar complement the beat. Now that beat does mutate, changing when you least expect it, made all the more sneaky with the hallmark Shellac repetition.And that's the key: repetition. Hypnotic, hammer-pounding, steady, repetition. It's like the simplicity of punk rock, taken to an extreme, yet still musical. It doesn't dazzle you with wanky solos, or self-consciously sappy lyrics. It strives to provide that "bulldozer advancing down the road" heaviness, coupled with a severely ironic, yet never pretentious, lyrical quality.It is a dream-come-true for those who appreciate the forceful minimalism of punk rock, yet it would not be classified as punk by any who hear it.
